docs.title: mpp-sdk documentation
docs.text: A Python SDK for designing, comparing, and deploying Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithms for photovoltaic systems.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• General Information - what the system is, the four SDK pillars, minimum PV theory, what pvlib contributes, and why the panels are wired in series.
  • Rationale - the design decisions behind the project.
  • Methodology - how the harnesses measure MPPT performance, what each metric means, the restart trigger policy, noise robustness, and the sim-to-real (PLECS / bench) comparison protocol.
  • Measurement Procedure - the checklist for capturing a curve, running a tilted series, and running a closed-loop run on the bench.

docs.title: Hardware & Boards
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi Setup - enable SPI, install the SDK, wire the Pico, start the workbench server and install the boot service.
  • Dual-Board Compatibility Guide - how the codebase seamlessly runs on both Raspberry Pi 5 and BeagleBone Black with automatic SPI bus selection and cross-version compatibility.
  • BeagleBone Black Setup Guide - step-by-step guide for flashing Debian 13 IoT, enabling the SPI1 overlay, wiring, and running mpp-sdk on the BeagleBone Black.
  • ADC Calibration - calibration procedure for the hardware analog frontend.

docs.title: Algorithm references
docs.text:
One page each, with the equations and references:

  • Perturb & Observe - classical hill-climbing baseline
  • Incremental Conductance - explicit at-the-MPP test
  • Fuzzy Logic - graduated-step local tracker
  • Scan-and-Track - global MPPT (scan + local refine)
  • Particle Swarm - global MPPT (population search)
  • Restart Policy - when a global tracker re-searches

The first three are local trackers (they get trapped on local maxima under partial shading); the last two are global methods that escape the trap.

Source and full roadmap: github.com/UTN-FRBA-2026-PF-EE-GP10/mpp_sdk.

docs.title: BeagleBone Black setup
docs.text: How to use a BeagleBone Black (BBB, Rev C) as the bench host instead of a Raspberry Pi. Only the BBB-specific steps are here. The shared steps are in the Raspberry Pi setup: install uv, clone the repository, uv sync --extra hardware --extra web, start the workbench, install the boot service.

docs.title: Prepare the board
docs.text:
1. Flash the Debian 13 (Trixie) IoT image for the AM335x to a microSD card. Use the image and the steps on the official BeagleBoard site (https://www.beagleboard.org/distros). The IoT image has no desktop.
  2. Hold the USER/BOOT button while you apply power. The board then boots from the SD card instead of the eMMC.
  3. Log in over ssh as <user> at <bbb-host>. Over USB the board is usually at 192.168.7.2. Change the default password.
  4. Run sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y.
  5. Optional: copy the OS to the 4 GB eMMC with sudo /opt/scripts/tools/eMMC/init-eMMC-flasher-v3.sh. It takes about 30 minutes. Remove the SD card after the board shuts down.
  6. Install uv as in the Pi setup. The BBB is 32-bit ARM (armv7l). Some wheels, for example numpy, may build from source. Install the build tools first: sudo apt install -y build-essential python3-dev libopenblas-dev gfortran.

docs.title: Enable SPI1
docs.text:
On the BBB the SPI pins need an overlay. A raspi-config toggle does not exist.

  1. HDMI uses the SPI1 pins. Add these lines to /boot/uEnv.txt:
disable_uboot_overlay_video=1
disable_uboot_overlay_audio=1
  1. On Debian 13 with kernel 6.x the overlays are under /boot/dtbs/$(uname -r)/overlays/. Merge the SPI1 overlay into the active device tree:
sudo fdtoverlay -i /boot/dtbs/$(uname -r)/am335x-boneblack-uboot.dtb \
                -o /boot/dtbs/$(uname -r)/am335x-boneblack-uboot.dtb \
                /boot/dtbs/$(uname -r)/overlays/BB-SPIDEV1-00A0.dtbo
  1. Load spidev at boot and give the user access without sudo:
echo spidev | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/spidev.conf
echo 'KERNEL=="spidev*", GROUP="dialout", MODE="0660"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/80-spidev.rules
  1. Reboot. Check that /dev/spidev1.0 and /dev/spidev1.1 exist.

The overlay change is permanent. If you set the pins with config-pin instead, the setting is lost at reboot. Then use a oneshot systemd unit that runs config-pin P9.28 spi_cs, P9.29 spi, P9.30 spi and P9.31 spi_sclk at boot.

docs.title: Wire the Pico
docs.text:
Both boards use 3.3 V logic. Wire them directly, with no level shifter. The Pico side is the same as for the Pi. Only the host side changes.

BBB pin BBB signal Direction Pico GPIO P9.31 SPI1_SCLK to Pico GPIO10 (SCK) P9.29 SPI1_D0 (MISO) from Pico GPIO11 (TX) P9.30 SPI1_D1 (MOSI) to Pico GPIO12 (RX) P9.28 SPI1_CS0 to Pico GPIO13 (CSn) P9.1 or P9.2 GND - GND

Optional SWD wires for flashing and logs from the BBB:

BBB pin Signal Pico pad P9.12 (GPIO 540) SWDIO SWDIO (right pad) P9.14 (GPIO 530) SWCLK SWCLK (left pad) P9.1 or P9.2 GND GND (middle pad)

The three SWD pads are at the bottom edge of the Pico, opposite the USB connector: SWCLK, GND, SWDIO from left to right.

docs.title: Test and run
docs.text:
1. Power the Pico board. Run uv run python scripts/spi_test.py --once. The line must show V_raw, I_raw, Vout_raw and a valid CRC.
  2. The SDK picks SPI bus 1 when /proc/device-tree/model names a BeagleBone. Use --bus 1 (spi_test.py) or --spi-bus 1 (server) to force it. In code use SpiMcuSource(bus=1, device=0).
  3. Start the workbench with uv run mpp-sdk curve-tracer-web. Open http://<bbb-host>:8000/.

docs.title: Flash the Pico over SWD from the BBB
docs.text:
You build on a PC and flash through the BBB. You do not unplug wires or press BOOTSEL.

  1. On the BBB run sudo apt install -y openocd.
  2. Write /etc/openocd/rp2040_swd.cfg on the BBB:
adapter driver sysfsgpio
sysfsgpio swdio_num 540
sysfsgpio swclk_num 530
transport select swd
source [find target/rp2040.cfg]
  1. On the PC, in firmware/pipico_board, run cargo build --release.
  2. Copy and flash:
scp target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/mpp-firmware <user>@<bbb-host>:/tmp/mpp-firmware.elf
ssh <user>@<bbb-host> "sudo openocd -f /etc/openocd/rp2040_swd.cfg -c 'program /tmp/mpp-firmware.elf verify reset exit'"

docs.title: Stream firmware logs (defmt over RTT)
docs.text:
1. On the PC run cargo install defmt-print.
  2. Write /etc/openocd/rp2040_rtt.cfg on the BBB:
bindto 0.0.0.0
adapter driver sysfsgpio
sysfsgpio swdio_num 540
sysfsgpio swclk_num 530
transport select swd
source [find target/rp2040.cfg]
init
poll off
rtt setup 0x20000000 0x40000 "SEGGER RTT"
rtt polling_interval 1000
rtt start
rtt server start 9999 0
  • poll off stops the continuous core polling. Without it, the SWD traffic wakes the gpio-manager service and uses 100 % of the single CPU core.
  • rtt polling_interval 1000 polls the buffer once per second. This matches the 1 Hz log rate and keeps the CPU at about 10-15 %.
  • Start it with low priority: sudo nice -n 19 openocd -f /etc/openocd/rp2040_rtt.cfg.
  • On the PC, from the repository root:
nc <bbb-host> 9999 | defmt-print -e firmware/pipico_board/target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/mpp-firmware

docs.title: Differences from the Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
What Raspberry Pi BBB Enable SPI raspi-config Overlay and HDMI disabled SPI device /dev/spidev0.0 (bus 0) /dev/spidev1.0 (bus 1) SPI pins Header pins 19, 21, 23, 24 P9.28 to P9.31 SWD pins BCM 24, 25 P9.12 (SWDIO), P9.14 (SWCLK) SpiMcuSource bus=0, device=0 bus=1, device=0 Algorithm and firmware changes none none

The BBB has a 1 GHz Cortex-A8 and 512 MB RAM. It is slower than a Pi 5 for plots, the workbench and heavy harness runs. The control loop is not affected: it is one step(V, I) call and one SPI exchange.

docs.title: Dual-Board Compatibility Guide: Raspberry Pi 5 & BeagleBone Black
docs.text: This document details the cross-platform changes implemented in mpp-sdk to ensure seamless, single-codebase operation on both the Raspberry Pi 5 and the BeagleBone Black (BBB) without maintaining separate branches or modifying code when swapping hardware.

docs.title: 1. Summary of Architectural Differences
docs.text: Feature Raspberry Pi 5 BeagleBone Black (Rev C) How It Is Handled Architecture 64-bit ARM (aarch64) 32-bit ARM (armv7l) Standard Python / pure POSIX paths Default Linux Distribution Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm / Trixie) Debian 13 (Trixie) IoT uv installs Python 3.14 on both SPI Interface File /dev/spidev0.0 (SPI0 CE0) /dev/spidev1.0 (SPI1 CS0) Board model check at startup Default SPI Bus Index bus = 0 bus = 1 1 when /proc/device-tree/model names a BeagleBone, else 0 Logic Levels 3.3 V CMOS 3.3 V CMOS Direct pin-to-pin wiring to RP2040 Pico (no shifter) RP2040 Firmware Unchanged Unchanged Same SPI slave protocol (12-byte frame + CRC-8)

docs.title: 2. What changes per board
docs.text:
• SPI bus. scripts/curve_tracer_server.py and scripts/spi_test.py read /proc/device-tree/model. A BeagleBone uses bus 1, all other boards use bus 0. --spi-bus (server) or --bus (spi_test.py) overrides it.
  • Python. Both boards run Python 3.14, installed by uv. The Debian 13 system Python (3.13) is not supported.
  • 204 routes. The server routes that return 204 No Content return an explicit empty Response. This works on all FastAPI versions.
  • Firmware. No change. The SPI protocol is the same on both boards.

docs.title: 3. Hardware Wiring Reference
docs.text:
The host SPI pins connect to the RP2040 Pico (acting as SPI slave) using 3.3V logic on both boards:

Raspberry Pi 5 (GPIO Header)       RP2040 Pico (Slave)      BeagleBone Black (P9 Header)
─────────────────────────────      ───────────────────      ────────────────────────────
GPIO 11 (SPI0_SCLK)          ──►   GPIO 14 (SCK)       ◄──  P9.31 (SPI1_SCLK)
GPIO 9  (SPI0_MISO)          ◄──   GPIO 11 (TX/MISO)   ──►  P9.29 (SPI1_D0 / MISO)
GPIO 10 (SPI0_MOSI)          ──►   GPIO 12 (RX/MOSI)   ◄──  P9.30 (SPI1_D1 / MOSI)
GPIO 8  (SPI0_CE0)           ──►   GPIO 13 (CSn)       ◄──  P9.28 (SPI1_CS0)
GND                          ───   GND                 ───  P9.1 or P9.2 (GND)

docs.title: 4. Verification
docs.text:
• uv run pytest passes on both boards.
  • Both boards run scripts/spi_test.py and the curve-tracer server (with or without --demo).

docs.title: General Information
docs.text: A starting point for anyone new to the project. It explains what the system does, how the pieces fit together, what pvlib contributes, and the minimum PV theory needed to be productive.

docs.title: What this project is
docs.text:
mpp-sdk is a Python SDK for designing, comparing, and deploying Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithms for photovoltaic (PV) systems. It backs an Electronics Engineering thesis. The final deliverable is an MPPT algorithm running on a microcontroller, validated end to end through the same codebase that compares it against classical methods.

The guiding principle: the same controller code runs in simulation today and on real hardware tomorrow, unchanged. Only the underlying source is swapped.

docs.title: The physical system
docs.text:
PV panels  ──►  SEPIC converter  ──►  load
   (2× Hissuma      (DC-DC stage,         (resistor /
    in series)       duty-cycle D)          battery)
        ▲                  ▲
        │ V, I             │ PWM duty
        └──────────────────┴──► RP2040 (firmware, Rust)
                                    │ SPI
                                    ▼
                            Host/sbc (Python SDK)
  • Panels: two Hissuma PSF10MONO (10 W each) in series. Series wiring is deliberate: it is what makes partial-shading experiments meaningful (see Why series below).
  • SEPIC converter: a DC-DC stage whose duty cycle \(D\) sets the panel operating point. SEPIC is the choice because the panel MPP voltage can sit above or below the load voltage, with no change in topology.
  • RP2040 (Raspberry Pi Pico): drives the converter PWM, reads voltage and current (an INA229 power monitor over SPI, plus an INA281 sense amplifier into the on-chip ADC as an analog cross-check), and talks to the Host/sbc over SPI. Firmware is in Rust. It is also the deployment target for the final algorithm.
  • Host/sbc: hosts the Python SDK, and the algorithm during hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing. See AGENTS.md for the target model.

docs.title: The four SDK pillars
docs.text:
The library is decoupled into four pillars, each verifiable in isolation:

Pillar Package What it provides Models mpp_sdk.models Panel I-V models (ideal, pvlib-backed, string) Converters mpp_sdk.converters Power-stage models (SEPICConverter) Algorithms mpp_sdk.algorithms MPPT controllers (PerturbAndObserve, FuzzyLogic, …) IO mpp_sdk.io Hardware-abstraction seam (SignalSource)

The seam is SignalSource: an algorithm only ever calls read() → (V, I) and write(D). Whether that is a simulation or a real board is invisible to it.

docs.title: Minimum PV theory
docs.text:
A solar panel's current-voltage (I-V) relationship follows the single-diode model:

\[I(V) = I_\text{ph} - I_0\left(e^{V/(n V_t)} - 1\right) - \frac{V + I R_s}{R_{sh}},\]

where \(I_\text{ph}\) is the light-generated (photo) current, \(I_0\) the diode saturation current, \(R_s, R_{sh}\) the series/shunt resistances, and \(V_t\) the thermal voltage. The key consequences:

  • Short circuit: at \(V=0\), \(I \approx I_\text{sc}\) (proportional to irradiance).
  • Open circuit: at \(I=0\), \(V = V_\text{oc}\) (falls with temperature).
  • Maximum power point (MPP): the single \((V_\text{mp}, I_\text{mp})\) where \(P = VI\) peaks. MPPT's whole job is to find and hold this point as irradiance and temperature change.

Power curve: \(P(V) = V\cdot I(V)\) is bell-shaped with one peak - under uniform light. The MPP moves with conditions, which is why a closed-loop tracker is needed rather than a fixed operating point.

docs.title: What pvlib contributes
docs.text:
pvlib is the de-facto open-source library for PV performance modelling. It provides validated single- and two-diode I-V solvers, temperature/irradiance models, and the bishop88 partial-shading method.

pvlib does not provide closed-loop MPPT controllers, time-stepping control simulation, or any hardware abstraction. It returns the MPP for a given panel and environment. It does not discover the MPP from a stream of \((V, I)\) measurements, the way a controller does.

mpp-sdk fills that gap and adopts pvlib rather than competing with it. PvlibPanelModel wraps pvlib's solver behind the SDK's PanelModel interface, so controllers get validated panel physics with no re-implementation. We fit the De Soto 5-parameter model from the panel's datasheet values (Voc, Isc, Vmp, Imp, and temperature coefficients).

docs.title: Why series (partial shading)
docs.text:
Two panels in series share one current. When one is shaded, its bypass diode conducts over part of the curve. That produces a multi-peak P-V curve. Classical trackers (P&O, InCond, fuzzy) follow the local gradient and can get stuck on a local maximum, losing power. This is why a global MPPT method (scan-and-track) is needed, and the series string is what lets us demonstrate it. Two panels in parallel would keep a single-peak curve and hide the effect.

Hardware limits for the series string: \(V_\text{oc} \approx 34\) V, \(I_\text{sc} \approx 0.79\) A - the SEPIC is designed for \(\le 40\) V, \(\le 1\) A.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
uv sync --extra pvlib            # install with the pvlib adapter
uv run harness/compare_static.py # full-sun vs partial-shade comparison
uv run harness/animate.py --shade --duty 0.1   # watch the local-maximum trap
uv run harness/compare_cyclic.py # the ranking measurement (chaotic shading)
uv run harness/compare_bank.py   # the sim-to-real test-case bank
uv run harness/compare_noise.py  # robustness vs measurement noise
uv run mpp-sdk compare-measured  # grade algorithms against a captured curve
uv run pytest -q                 # run the test suite

Every script above is also reachable through one dispatcher - uv run mpp-sdk --help lists all of them (uv run mpp-sdk compare-static, uv run mpp-sdk animate --shade, ...); each stays directly runnable on its own too, as shown here.

Every compare_* script prints a "how to read the metrics" guide before its table. See docs/methodology.md for the full measurement methodology, docs/algorithms/ for one-page references on each MPPT method, and docs/rationale.md for the design decisions behind the project.

The web workbench (uv run mpp-sdk curve-tracer-web) captures real panel I-V curves and can drive closed-loop runs on the bench. See docs/measurement_procedure.md for the capture checklist.

docs.title: Measurement procedure
docs.text: A checklist for running a bench measurement session: capturing one curve, running a tilted series, and a closed-loop run. See README.md's Quickstart to install the web extra first.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Never expose the server to the internet or an untrusted network. It has no login and no access control. Anyone who can reach it can drive the SEPIC converter. Keep it on the bench network only, or reachable through a VPN.
  • The curve tracer's bleed path dissipates power in Q3 (a linear MOSFET). Give it a heatsink and watch its temperature if you run sweeps back-to-back - see firmware/pipico_board/README.md's "Curve tracer" section.
  • A closed-loop run has few on-target cutoffs. The firmware sets duty to 0 when:
  • the Pi sends no frame for about 500 ms,
  • the Pi sends only frames that fail their CRC for 500 ms,
  • the INA229 gives no new reading for 50 ms,
  • the panel current or a voltage goes above the hardware cutoff (default 1.0 A and 40 V). The cutoff latches; clear it with "Reset Tripped Cutoff" in the workbench. A host can only lower these limits.

The Pi side aborts the run when readings stay above v_max/i_max, when the converter output stays above v_out_max, or when the SPI link drops. This protection works only while the controlling process (the workbench server, or run-algorithm) runs. - Always put a load on the converter output before a run. With a light or missing load the SEPIC output climbs far above the panel voltage. - Choose the load from the panel curve: - The panel looks like R_in = Vmp / Imp at its MPP. A load near that value puts the MPP near duty 0.5. Two Hissuma panels in series are about 80 Ohm. - Output voltage is about sqrt(P x R_load). Keep it below v_out_max (25 V), or the run aborts. At 80 Ohm that means less than about 7 W. - Keep the panel power below 80 % of the resistor rating.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• [ ] Board wired and powered. See firmware/pipico_board/README.md's "GPIO Assignments" section for the pinout.
  • [ ] Firmware flashed with FIRMWARE_MODE = MppTracker (the default - check firmware/pipico_board/src/main.rs if unsure).
  • [ ] Panel(s) connected and getting light. A sweep on a dark panel aborts - see firmware/pipico_board/README.md's "Curve tracer" section, "Auto-range", for why.
  • [ ] mpp-sdk curve-tracer-web running (real board), or mpp-sdk curve-tracer-web --demo (practice run, any machine, no board - useful for rehearsing this checklist first).

docs.title: Start the workbench at boot (optional)
docs.text:
Run this once on the host SBC, from the repo checkout:

scripts/install_workbench_service.sh
  • It installs and starts the mpp-workbench systemd service. The server then starts at every boot, with no PC and no ssh session.
  • Open http://<host-ip>:8000/ from any device on the bench network, for example a phone.
  • The server does not need the Pico at start. The connection pill shows an error until the board answers, then changes to PICO connected.
  • Nothing drives the converter until you start a sweep or a run.
  • Stop the service before you start the server by hand. Both use port 8000 and the SPI link.
Task Command Status systemctl status mpp-workbench Log journalctl -u mpp-workbench -f Restart (after git pull and uv sync) sudo systemctl restart mpp-workbench Stop until next boot sudo systemctl stop mpp-workbench Remove scripts/install_workbench_service.sh --remove

docs.title: Capture one curve
docs.text:
1. Open http://<host-ip>:8000/ (or http://localhost:8000/ for --demo). The workbench opens on Measure.
  2. Check the connection pill, top right. It also doubles as the capture mode menu:
  3. PICO connected: a real board, live sweeps. Use this for an actual measurement.
  4. Replay on the board: a real board, but the "Replay curve" buttons replay a curve already stored in the firmware instead of measuring one. Only selectable while a board is linked.
  5. Demo: no board at all, bundled sample data, nothing saved. Leave it on PICO connected for a real capture.
  6. Under "Capturing under:", select the tab that matches this capture: Baseline here (or Tilted - see "The tilted-panel procedure" below).
  7. Click Start Measurement. Wait for the curve to finish plotting - a few seconds, since the sweep auto-ranges and takes 20 points.
  8. Fill in the save form: a label (a short description - suggest a convention like "<date> <condition>", e.g. "2026-09-08 baseline lamp 30cm") and optional notes (lamp distance, ambient light, anything unusual). Panel A is fixed at 90 degrees and is not editable in the form. Leave panel B's tilt at 90 degrees for a baseline capture (both panels matching).
  9. Click Save curve. Confirm it appears in the "Saved curves" table below, and under Curves > Baseline in the sidebar.

docs.title: The tilted-panel procedure
docs.text:
Setup facts:

  • The array is two panels and a lamp. Light travels from 180 degrees toward 0 degrees. 90 degrees is vertical and faces the light, so 90 is the untilted reference, not zero.
  • Panel A is fixed at 90 degrees. It is the unshaded reference.
  • Panel B moves on a mount with five detents: 90, 70, 60, 45, 30 degrees. A lower number tilts B further from the light, so it gets less light.
  • One tilted capture and a full sweep of angles are the same setup. Both use one measurement kind, tilted. mpp-sdk compare-measured (see docs/methodology.md, "Measured curves") then grades an algorithm on a real partial-shading curve.

For a sweep of angles, repeat "Capture one curve" for each angle:

  1. Set panel B to the next detent by hand.
  2. Select the Tilted tab, not Baseline.
  3. Click Start Measurement.
  4. In the save form, pick the same angle for panel B. The selector allows only the five detents.
  5. Use one label prefix for the series, with the angle added, for example "2026-09-08 tilted 45deg".
  6. Keep the lighting and panel A the same for the whole series.
  7. Sweeps run back-to-back. See the Safety section about the Q3 heatsink.

After the series, run mpp-sdk compare-measured. It groups saved curves by measurement kind, so the series shows up together.

docs.title: Where the files land
docs.text: Captured curves live under data/curves/, one JSON file per sweep (git-ignored - see data/README.md). Closed-loop runs (below) live under data/runs/. Both directories can be overridden per-process (MPP_SDK_CURVE_DIR, MPP_SDK_RUN_DIR) - see data/README.md if you need that.

docs.title: Closed-loop runs
docs.text: A run drives the SEPIC continuously with a live algorithm, unlike the curve tracer's separate, bounded bleed path. See the Safety section above for what protects it.

docs.title: From the workbench
docs.text:
1. In Measure, click the Run an algorithm tab.
  2. Pick an Algorithm, and optionally a saved curve as Reference curve (grades the run against it; leave it as "None" to run ungraded).
  3. Leave Duration blank for the default (10 s), or set your own, up to the server's safety backstop (600 s). Starting duty cycle picks which maximum a local tracker hill-climbs to on a multi-peak curve. v_max/i_max/v_out_max default to 40 V / 0.9 A / 25 V and set the abort limits. A limit aborts the run only when readings stay above it for 5 readings in a row and at least 50 ms; a shorter streak is treated as a bad reading and skipped.
  4. Click Start run and confirm. This drives the real converter.
  5. Watch the live V/I/duty readouts and the operating point move on the reference curve. Click Stop run to end it early.
  6. When it finishes, click Open in player to review the saved run, or Start another run.

In --demo mode, or with Demo capture mode selected, the form starts a simulated run instead (against a demo curve or a built-in reference panel). No board is touched, and the workbench marks the result "simulated" throughout so it is never mistaken for a measurement.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Useful for scripted or headless captures:

  1. uv run mpp-sdk run-algorithm --algorithm "P&O" --duration-s 10 --label bench-check. By default this also sweeps and saves a ground-truth curve first (skip that with --no-sweep --curve <path> to reuse an existing capture). Prints a summary (steps captured, whether it aborted, the final V/I/D) and saves a run under data/runs/.
  2. uv run mpp-sdk plot-run (with no argument, plots the most recent run). Produces a figure with the P-V curve and the run's trajectory overlaid (colored by time), plus V/I/P time series.

Other flags: --v-max/--i-max/--v-out-max (narrow the 40 V / 0.9 A / 25 V default limits), --bus/--device/--speed-hz (SPI settings, same defaults as the other hardware scripts). Run mpp-sdk run-algorithm --help / mpp-sdk plot-run --help for the full list.

docs.title: Bench sessions
docs.text: A session is a checklist for one bench session: setup fields, a list of steps with a status, and curves and runs linked to those steps. A curve or run links into a step - it is never copied - so a session always shows the current state of your saved library.

docs.title: Start a session
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, open Sessions and click New session.
  2. Pick a template. The workbench suggests the one that matches your current setup mode (Single or Full).
  3. Type a title, e.g. "Panel A alone under the lamp". Fill in the setup fields - panel model, light source, load, ADC range - where they differ from the defaults.
  4. Click Create session. The workbench opens the new session.

docs.title: Fill in steps
docs.text:
Each step has a status: todo, done, failed, or skipped. Set it from the dropdown next to the step. Steps come in four kinds:

  • Check: mark it done once you have verified something, e.g. firmware configuration.
  • Number or text: type a value, e.g. Voc read off the panel label.
  • Curve: link one or more saved curves. Pick one from the list, or click Link most recent curve right after you save one.
  • Run: link one or more saved runs, the same way.

Notes are free text under each step, for anything the checklist itself does not capture.

docs.title: Repeats and statistics
docs.text:
• A curve or run step can ask for more than one repeat, for example 3 curves one after the other. The step shows "2 / 3 repeats".
  • With two or more linked, the workbench shows median, mean, standard deviation, min and max. For curves: Voc, Isc, P at MPP. For runs: held power, P over MPP_th, time to converge.
  • With one linked, it shows that value alone.

docs.title: Printing and downloads
docs.text:
• Expand all opens every linked chart. Use it before you print (Ctrl+P or Cmd+P). The workbench also expands them when the print dialog opens. Collapse all closes them.
  • Download JSON saves the session record.
  • Download Markdown saves a readable summary: each step, its value and notes, and the statistics.
  • Both downloads hold the session alone, without the linked curves and runs.

docs.title: Sharing a session file
docs.text:
A session file bundles curves and runs, and optionally the session, into one file. Someone else can open it with no board and no saved library.

Export from a session:

  1. Open the session and click Export session file.
  2. The file holds the session record and every linked curve and run. A linked item that was deleted is listed as missing.

Export loose curves or runs:

  1. In Curves or Runs, click Select and tick the items.
  2. Click Export N selected and type a title. The title is the file name. The file holds no session.

The browser downloads <title>.mppsession.json.

Open a file:

  1. Start mpp-sdk curve-tracer-web --demo on any machine.
  2. Click Open session in the header, or drag the file onto the page.
  3. A Viewing: <title> banner shows. Click Close to leave.

While you view a file:

  • Capture, starting a run, deleting and remeasuring are off. Nothing is sent to a server.
  • Curve and run views work as usual. The player reads the run samples from the file.
  • View session opens the session read-only, if the file has one.

A bad file (wrong format, too large, corrupted) shows an error. The current view stays as it was.

docs.title: Comparison methodology
docs.text: How the harness measures MPPT performance, what each number means, and how the simulation results will be reproduced on PLECS and on the bench. For the system overview see general_information.md; for design decisions, rationale.md.

docs.title: One idea behind every metric
docs.text: At every instant the panel has a best possible power, \(P_\text{mpp}\): the global maximum of the P-V curve for the current irradiance and temperature. Every metric compares what the controller actually captured against that ideal. The reference comes from the same panel model the simulation runs on (TabulatedPanel.mpp()). So the simulated world and the grading curve are identical, by construction.

docs.title: Five harnesses, five questions
docs.text:
Harness Question Replicable on hardware? compare_cyclic.py Which algorithm is better under realistic, changing shading? No, and it does not need to be (sim-only ranking) compare_bank.py Does the simulation predict reality? Yes: five simple scenarios, one shade cloth compare_noise.py How fast does each algorithm degrade with measurement noise? Indirectly (the bench has a fixed noise floor) compare_rescan.py What is the right rescan period? No (sim-only, feeds the trigger-policy figure) compare_seeds.py How seed-sensitive is the stochastic tracker? No (sim-only)

The split matters. A rich, chaotic, seeded schedule is ideal for ranking, but impossible to reproduce with a real sun. Bench scenarios must stay simple. One experiment cannot do both jobs well.

compare_static.py, compare_dynamic.py and animate.py predate the methodology and remain as smoke tests and demos.

docs.title: The metrics
docs.text:
• eta energy \(= \sum_k P_k \,/\, \sum_k P_{\text{mpp},k}\): captured energy over ideally-available energy across the whole run, with a time-varying reference (metrics.energy_efficiency). This is the headline energy bill. It is energy-weighted: deep-shade segments offer little energy, so failing them barely dents this number. Always read it together with the trap columns.
  • success / trapped: how many held conditions (plateaus) ended within 5 % of \(P_\text{mpp}\), and for the trapped ones, the settled fraction of available power (mean and worst). This is the honest pain number: when trapped, the controller delivers X % of what the panel could give.
  • re-acquisition: time from a condition change until the power returns inside the 5 % band and stays there. Local trackers re-acquire in ~10 ms, or never (trapped). Global trackers always re-acquire, but pay their search time, bounded by the rescan period.
  • Building blocks in mpp_sdk.metrics: tracking_efficiency, final_efficiency, settling_time, steady_state_ripple, overshoot, trap_depth. Each harness prints a plain-language guide before its table.

docs.title: Why global trackers need a trigger policy
docs.text:
A global search (full duty sweep, or a PSO pass) physically drives the converter across its range. Exploration costs energy, so it cannot run continuously. After the search, a local P&O holds the found peak. The open question is when to search again - it moves the results more than the choice of search itself does. Two mechanisms, both on the controller side and both fed only by \((V, I)\):

  1. Step detector (PowerChangeDetector, on by default): restart when \(|\Delta P|/P > 20\,\%\) for 3 consecutive control steps. The reference follows the power while it stays in band. It arms only once the power is stable after a search, so the converter's own recovery transient (the input capacitor recharging, panel-current-limited at low irradiance) cannot cause a restart loop. It fires on steps only.
  2. Periodic backstop (rescan_period): re-search every \(N\) tracking steps, unconditionally. This covers the step detector's blind spot: changes that reshape the curve without moving the tracked power, which includes every slow ramp into partial shading. Its cost is one search per period (a few percent of energy at 1 s). Its benefit is bounding the worst-case trapped time to the period.

Measured on the cyclic schedule: local trackers trap in roughly half the shaded plateaus, at 44-66 % of available power. The configured global trackers cut traps to a handful, at the price of up to ~1 s re-acquisition when only the backstop can free them. The deployed period (1000 steps) is not a guess: an expected-loss model derives an optimum \(P^\star \approx 1035\), which lands on the empirically measured best (eta peaks at 95.0 % at period 1000). See algorithms/restart_policy.md for the full derivation.

docs.title: Measurement noise
docs.text:
Real sense chains are noisy, and clean-sim numbers flatter the simple methods. NoisySource adds seeded Gaussian noise to the \((V, I)\) samples the controller sees. The plant stays clean; grading uses true power. The noise is specified as a fraction of the hardware full scale (40 V / 1 A).

Why the cliff happens: fixed-step P&O decides direction from the sign of the power change across a duty perturbation. Near the MPP that change is tiny. Once per-sample noise exceeds it, the decision is a coin flip and the tracker random-walks away (the classical step-size design constraint, Femia et al. 2005). On this rig the cliff sits between 0.25 % and 0.5 % of full scale. Global searches keep a ~60 % floor at levels that reduce P&O to ~19 %, because each sweep yanks the operating point back near the peak.

docs.title: Sim-to-real: the three-layer comparison
docs.text:
Closed-loop waveforms from different environments are never compared directly. The claim is split, so a disagreement points at the broken layer:

  1. Plant vs plant (validates DynamicSimulatedSource against the PLECS switched model): replay the same recorded duty sequence open-loop into both and compare \(V(t), I(t)\). The panel enters PLECS as a lookup table exported by scripts/export_iv_plecs.py, so both simulators share the same curve by construction.
  2. Controller vs controller (validates a port, PLECS C-Script or the RP2040 firmware, against the Python reference): replay recorded \((V, I)\) traces through both and compare the emitted duty sequences step by step. Deterministic algorithms only.
  3. Closed loop: run the test-case bank in each environment and compare the metrics tables within documented tolerances.

compare_bank.py dumps a \((t, V, I, D)\) CSV per run, to feed layers 1 and 2. On the bench, the scenarios map to one shade cloth of ~30 % transmission (cover on, cover off, steady shade), plus the controller's configured start duty for the Voc-side trap case. The ground truth \(P_\text{mpp}\) comes from a calibration duty sweep with the condition held - the rig is its own instrument.

docs.title: Measured curves: replaying real panel data
docs.text:
mpp_sdk.curves captures I-V sweeps from the curve tracer. RP2040 firmware sweeps the bench panel's whole voltage range and streams the result to the Pi over SPI (see frontend/README.md for the web workbench). MeasuredPanel implements the same PanelModel interface as any synthetic model. So the comparison harness (mpp-sdk compare-measured) runs the full algorithm bank against an actual captured curve, with zero algorithm changes. This goes a step past layer 1's "same curve, both simulators" claim above: it replaces the panel model with what the panel actually did, not a model of it.

This lets partial-shading scenarios (one panel physically tilted or shaded relative to the other) be graded against the array's real P-V shape, instead of an inferred multi-modal curve, before any algorithm is committed to firmware. See docs/measurement_procedure.md for the bench capture checklist, including the tilt convention and closed-loop hardware runs (RunRecord, mpp-sdk run-algorithm).

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Every stochastic element is seeded: the cyclic schedule, the PSO swarm, the noise stream. Re-running any harness reproduces its numbers exactly. Changing a seed is a deliberate, visible act. Every figure in the paper must be regenerable from a command. Stochastic algorithms are reported as mean ± std over 30 seeds (compare_seeds.py), never a single seed.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi setup
docs.text: How to prepare a Raspberry Pi as the host of the bench. It runs the workbench server and talks to the Pico over SPI. For a BeagleBone Black, see the BeagleBone Black setup.

docs.title: Set up the Pi
docs.text:
1. Install Raspberry Pi OS and make sure you can log in over ssh: ssh <user>@<pi-host>.
  2. Enable the SPI interface:
  3. Run sudo raspi-config, then Interface Options, then SPI, then Yes.
  4. Reboot.
  5. Check that /dev/spidev0.0 exists.
  6. Install git and uv. Follow the uv install page, then check that uv is on the PATH.
  7. Get the repository:

cd mpp_sdk

  2. Connect the Pi SPI0 pins to the Pico SPI1 pins. The Pico is the slave.

docs.title: Check the power
docs.text:
1. Run vcgencmd get_throttled on the Pi.
  2. The result must be 0x0.
  3. Any other value means under-voltage or throttling. Under-voltage can stall SPI and abort runs. Fix the supply before you measure:
  4. Use a supply rated for the Pi.
  5. Give the lamp and other loads their own supply.

docs.title: Start the workbench server
docs.text:
1. Run the server from the repository:
uv run mpp-sdk curve-tracer-web

The first start is slow. Wait up to a minute. 2. Open http://<pi-host>:8000/ from any device on the bench network. 3. The server does not need the Pico at start. The connection pill shows an error until the board answers, then it shows PICO connected. 4. The server returns 403 if the browser uses a host name it does not know. IP addresses, localhost, the Pi's own name and <name>.local always work. For any other name, start the server with --allowed-host <name> (repeat the option for more names). 5. The server picks SPI bus 0 on a Raspberry Pi. Use --spi-bus to change it. 6. To try the workbench with no board, add --demo.

docs.title: Lamp
docs.text:
The server switches the lamp dimmer through the Pico. The board switches mains: read hardware/dimmer/README.md before bench work.

  • GET /api/dimmer returns the status: state (off, on, tripped, unavailable), power, window left, budget, and the dimmer flags.
  • POST /api/dimmer takes power (fraction 0 to 1) or alpha_deg (0 to 180), plus max_on_s (default 30, at most 120). It returns the status.
  • POST /api/dimmer/off switches the lamp off. It works in every state.
  • --lamp-max-power X caps the power the API accepts (0 < X <= 1, default 1.0). A higher request gets 422. An angle is capped by the power it gives.

Safety model:

  • The lamp is off at idle and after boot.
  • Every "on" is a window: the host switches the lamp off when it ends.
  • A window is at most 120 s. The dimmer also counts on time: at 120 s it trips and forces the lamp off. It cools 1 s per 1 s.
  • While tripped, every "on" gets 409. It clears when the dimmer has cooled to 60 s and the host has sent an OFF after the trip.
  • Lamp commands do not wait for runs or sweeps, so Off works during a run.
  • The lamp is switched off when the server stops. With --demo a simulated dimmer with the same rules is used.

Lamp only around a measurement:

  • POST /api/start-sweep and POST /api/runs/start take an optional lamp object: {"power": 0.3, "warmup_s": 3}. Use alpha_deg instead of power (exactly one). warmup_s is 0 to 30 s, default 3. The same power rules and --lamp-max-power cap as POST /api/dimmer apply.
  • The server switches the lamp on, waits warmup_s, starts the measurement, and switches the lamp off when it ends. It also switches off on Stop, on an abort, on an error, on a sweep that never reports, and when the server stops.
  • The lamp is on for warmup_s + duration + 5 s margin. That total must be at most 110 s, because the dimmer trips at 120 s. For a sweep the duration is taken as 15 s, the time the server waits for a sweep to report. A longer total gets 422 and the message gives the numbers.
  • Refusals, all before anything is switched on or started: 409 when the dimmer is tripped or its budget is smaller than the total (the message gives the seconds to wait), 503 when the dimmer link is not confirmed.
  • lamp_phase in GET /api/runs/live and GET /api/data is null (no lamp option), warming, measuring or off. lamp_warmup_left_s counts down while warming.
  • Stop during the warm-up cancels the run and switches the lamp off. The measurement never starts.
  • A manual POST /api/dimmer/off ends the lamp phase (off). During the warm-up the measurement is cancelled. During the measurement it goes on, but in the dark. A newer manual window is never switched off by the step.
  • A run that used the lamp keeps lamp (power or alpha_deg, and warmup_s) in its record settings.

The server has no login. Keep it on the bench network. See the safety notes in the measurement procedure.

docs.text:
1. Run this once on the Pi, from the repository, as the user that owns it:
scripts/install_workbench_service.sh
  1. The script asks for sudo once. It writes and starts the mpp-workbench systemd service. No path or user name is stored in the repository.
  2. Stop any server you started by hand first. Both use port 8000 and the SPI link.

docs.title: Restart safely
docs.text:
1. Wait until the workbench is idle: no sweep and no run in progress. A restart during a run loses the run.
  2. After git pull and uv sync, restart the service: sudo systemctl restart mpp-workbench.
  3. For a server started by hand, stop it with Ctrl+C in its terminal. If it runs in the background, find its process with pgrep -f "[m]pp-sdk curve-tracer-web" and stop it with kill. Do not run pkill -f "mpp-sdk curve-tracer-web" in an ssh command string. It matches its own shell.
  4. Do not keep a debug probe attached during sweeps or runs. It can make the Pico reject Pi frames. Attach it only between runs.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The why behind the project's design decisions. For how the system works, see general_information.md; for what each algorithm does, see docs/algorithms/.

docs.title: Why a control SDK at all
docs.text: The Python PV ecosystem has a strong modelling library (pvlib) but no shared control library. Most MPPT comparison work in the literature uses MATLAB/Simulink, with code that is rarely released and per-paper bespoke metrics. That makes cross-paper comparison and sim-to-real validation hard to reproduce. mpp-sdk is the missing piece: a uniform MPPTAlgorithm.step(V, I) → D interface, so adding a controller is a one-file change, plus a comparison harness that measures every algorithm the same way.

docs.title: Why the hardware-abstraction seam
docs.text:
The single most important design decision is the SignalSource seam. An algorithm only sees read() → (V, I) and write(D). This buys three things:

  1. Sim-to-real parity. The same controller code runs against a simulated panel and against the real SEPIC board. There is no separate "simulation version" and "hardware version" to drift apart.
  2. Independent verification. Each pillar (models, converters, algorithms, IO) is tested in isolation. A test that needs two pillars at once means the abstraction leaks - fix the seam, not the test.
  3. A natural MCU deployment target. The seam sits exactly where the firmware boundary falls: from the Pi's point of view, the RP2040 is a SignalSource.

docs.title: Why SEPIC
docs.text: A SEPIC (Single-Ended Primary-Inductance Converter) can step the panel voltage up or down. The panel MPP voltage can sit on either side of the load voltage, with no change in topology. For a demonstrator that sweeps a wide irradiance range, this avoids redesigning the power stage for each operating condition. The reflected input resistance \(R_\text{eff}(D) = R_\text{load}\left(\tfrac{1-D}{D}\right)^2\) is monotonic in the duty cycle. That gives a clean, single-valued mapping from \(D\) to the operating point.

docs.title: Continuous vs discontinuous conduction mode (CCM/DCM)
docs.text:
In ideal Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM), the voltage transfer ratio is strictly \(V_\text{out} = V_\text{in} \cdot \frac{D}{1-D}\). On the physical bench, the converter runs in Discontinuous Conduction Mode (DCM) at light loads (high load resistance). In DCM, the inductor current falls to zero within each switching cycle. That breaks the continuous flux-balance assumption and pushes the output voltage above the ideal CCM ratio.

During early bench bring-up, at a fixed commanded duty \(D = 0.5\) and \(V_\text{in} = 3.3\text{ V}\), the measured output voltage varied a lot with load:

  • ~3.3 V into a 10 \(\Omega\) load - matches the ideal CCM ratio \(3.3 \cdot \frac{0.5}{1-0.5} = 3.3\text{ V}\).
  • ~6.0 V into a 10 k\(\Omega\) load - DCM boost behavior under light load.
  • ~7.0 V open-circuit - the unloaded DCM ceiling.

Knowing this regime transition matters for hardware validation and characterization.

docs.title: Firmware operating modes
docs.text:
To simplify converter characterization on the bench, with no host-side control loop needed, the RP2040 firmware has two operating modes (FIRMWARE_MODE):

  • FirmwareMode::MppTracker: the RP2040 acts as a pure hardware I/O proxy. The algorithm on the Host/sbc reads \((V, I)\) and commands the duty cycle \(D\) over SPI. A link-lost watchdog forces \(D = 0\) if SPI communication drops for more than 500 ms.
  • FirmwareMode::PowerSupply: the RP2040 runs as an autonomous closed-loop bench power supply. It regulates output voltage \(V_\text{out}\) to a fixed setpoint (POWER_SUPPLY_VOUT_MV, 5 V) using on-chip ADC feedback (MEAS_ADC_VOUT_MV). In this mode the local regulator keeps running even if the host SPI connection drops.

For implementation details, setpoint configuration, and watchdog behavior - including the ClosedLoop feed-forward-plus-trim algorithm - see firmware/pipico_board/README.md's "Operating Modes" section. That file lives outside docs/, so it is linked directly on GitHub.

docs.title: Why these algorithms, in this order
docs.text:
1. P&O - the baseline every MPPT paper compares against. Fixed-step, minimal state, trivial to port to an MCU.
  2. Incremental Conductance - the other classical method. It has an explicit "at-the-MPP" condition that reduces steady-state oscillation.
  3. Fuzzy logic - a local tracker with a graduated step. It shows that the speed/oscillation trade-off can be eased without a panel model. It is not global, and saying so plainly is part of the contribution.
  4. Scan-and-track and Particle Swarm Optimization - the genuine global MPPT methods, needed to escape the local maxima that partial shading creates. Scan-and-track is deterministic, and the easiest to bound in static RAM and defend mathematically. PSO is the popular population-based alternative. Both ship so the paper can compare them, but scan-and-track is the leading candidate for the MCU port.

The order matters: each algorithm needs at least one predecessor to compare against, and the metrics only make sense once several controllers run side by side.

docs.title: Why a dynamic source, not just static
docs.text:
The simplest simulation jumps instantly to the operating point: a snapshot, not a trajectory. To see how long an algorithm takes, whether it overshoots, and how it oscillates, the source models the SEPIC input capacitor:

\[C\frac{dV}{dt} = I_\text{panel}(V) - \frac{V}{R_\text{eff}(D)}.\]

DynamicSimulatedSource integrates this each control step. This is still a quasi-static electrical model, with no switching ripple. Switching- level fidelity is PLECS's job - it simulates the converter cycle by cycle. The two are complementary: the SDK validates the algorithm, PLECS validates the hardware.

docs.title: Why a restart policy instead of a smarter detector
docs.text: Once a global tracker hands off to its local stage, it is blind to new peaks. So something must decide when to search again. We use two deliberately simple mechanisms (see methodology.md): a step detector on \(|\Delta P|/P\) for abrupt changes, and a periodic re-search for everything the detector cannot see (slow ramps, power-preserving peak moves). The split is honest about what the controller can know: with only \((V, I)\) at one operating point, gradual curve reshaping is provably invisible. So the right tool is a bounded-cost backstop, not a cleverer detector. Both mechanisms need only a few scalars of state, which keeps them inside the MCU portability budget.

docs.title: Why noise lives in a source wrapper
docs.text: Measurement noise belongs to the acquisition chain, not the plant or the controller. NoisySource wraps any SignalSource and perturbs only what the controller sees. That keeps models and algorithms free of noise flags, and makes the noise level an explicit, seeded experiment parameter. The same wrapper doubles as a bench sanity check: measure the real sense chain's sigma, run the harness at that level, and the simulated degradation should bracket the measured one.

docs.title: Why every curve and run records where it came from
docs.text: A replayed or simulated curve looks exactly like a real measurement once it is saved as JSON. The same is true for a closed-loop run: a trace from SimulatedSource looks like one from the real SEPIC board. Grading an algorithm against data that is not what it claims to be would be a silent, uncorrectable error in the results. So CurveRecord.source and RunRecord.source tag where the data came from (hardware, firmware-replay, simulated, or unknown for curves; hardware, simulated, or unknown for runs). The web server stamps this field itself; it is never taken from a client request, so a client cannot mislabel its own data as real.

docs.title: Why tabulated panels in the harness
docs.text: PvString solves a nested bisection through a pvlib-backed solver - far too slow to call thousands of times in a dynamic run. TabulatedPanel samples the I-V curve once and interpolates after that. This makes the dynamic and animated harnesses fast enough to use, with no change to the physics the algorithm sees.

docs.title: On the use of AI
docs.text: The project uses LLM assistance as a deliberate productivity choice, under an explicit policy (see README.md, "On the use of AI"): every change is human-reviewed and tested, and the human author stays accountable for correctness. The framework and scaffolding are AI-leveraged so the team's limited hours go to the original contributions: hardware design, algorithm analysis, and experimental validation.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
Adaptive-step P&O keeps the direction rule of Perturb & Observe. It changes the step size \(\Delta D\) at each call:

  • Far from the MPP the power slope is large, so the step grows.
  • Near the MPP the slope is small, so the step shrinks.

This removes the fixed-step trade-off: fast convergence and low ripple at the same time.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The step is proportional to the relative power slope, clamped to a range:

\[\Delta D_k = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(g\,\frac{|\Delta P_k|}{\Delta D_{k-1}\,P_k},\;\Delta D_\min,\;\Delta D_\max\right)\]
  • \(|\Delta P_k| / \Delta D_{k-1}\) estimates \(|dP/dD|\) from the last perturbation.
  • Dividing by \(P_k\) makes the gain \(g\) independent of the panel power rating.
  • At the MPP, \(dP/dD = 0\), so the step falls to \(\Delta D_\min\). This value sets the steady-state ripple.
  • \(\Delta D_\max\) limits the speed far from the MPP.

docs.title: SEPIC sign convention
docs.text:
The direction rule is the same as for fixed-step P&O. Raising \(D\) lowers the panel voltage, so:

  • \(\Delta P\,\Delta V > 0\): decrease \(D\).
  • \(\Delta P\,\Delta V < 0\): increase \(D\).
  • \(\Delta P = 0\): hold.
\[D_{k+1} = D_k - \operatorname{sign}(\Delta P\,\Delta V)\,\Delta D_k\]

On the first call the controller records \((V, P)\) and moves up by \(\Delta D_\min\).

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• Ripple: set by \(\Delta D_\min\), not by \(\Delta D_\max\).
  • Speed: set by \(\Delta D_\max\) and the gain \(g\). A larger \(g\) reaches \(\Delta D_\max\) closer to the MPP.
  • Noise: the slope estimate uses one pair of samples. Noise can raise the step near the MPP. Keep \(g\) small on noisy measurements.
  • Partial shading: it follows the local gradient, so it can stay on a local maximum, like fixed-step P&O.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
mpp_sdk.AdaptivePerturbAndObserve(initial_duty, min_step, max_step, gain, min_duty, max_duty).

  • State: last \(V\), last \(P\), last step and the duty.
  • step() uses no loops and no libraries, so it runs on an MCU.
  • last_step gives the size of the most recent perturbation.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
A fuzzy-logic controller climbs the same hill as P&O, but replaces the fixed step with a graduated one obtained from linguistic rules: far from the MPP it takes large steps, near the MPP it takes small ones. This eases the speed/oscillation trade-off without an explicit model of the panel.

It remains a local tracker: it is trapped on local maxima under partial shading, so it is not a global MPPT method on its own.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Two normalized inputs are computed each step:

\[E = \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V} \quad(\text{power-voltage slope}), \qquad \Delta E = E_k - E_{k-1}.\]

\(E\) is the gradient \(dP/dV\): \(E>0\) means left of the MPP, \(E=0\) at it, \(E<0\) right of it. \(\Delta V \approx 0\) would make \(E\) blow up, so the implementation defines \(E=0\) in that case instead of dividing; the rule table then falls back to the ZE row, so the step depends only on \(\Delta E\), not on holding outright. Each input is scaled and clamped to \([-1,1]\):

\[\hat{E} = \operatorname{clip}\!\Big(\frac{E}{s_E},\,-1,\,1\Big), \qquad \hat{E}_\Delta = \operatorname{clip}\!\Big(\frac{\Delta E}{s_{\Delta E}},\,-1,\,1\Big).\]

docs.title: Fuzzification
docs.text:
Each input is mapped onto five triangular sets (NB, NS, ZE, PS, PB) with centres at \(\{-1,-0.5,0,0.5,1\}\) and half-width \(0.5\):

\[\mu_i(x) = \max\!\Big(0,\; 1 - \frac{|x - c_i|}{0.5}\Big).\]

docs.title: Rule base and inference
docs.text:
A \(5\times5\) Mamdani rule table assigns an output singleton \(r_{ij}\) (a duty step in \([-1,1]\)) to each combination of input sets. Because \(\Delta D\) must oppose \(E\) (SEPIC: raise \(V \Rightarrow\) lower \(D\)), the table is built so that large positive \(E\) yields a large negative \(\Delta D\), and vice-versa.

Rule weights use the product of memberships, \(w_{ij} = \mu_i(\hat{E})\,\mu_j(\hat{E}_\Delta)\).

docs.title: Defuzzification
docs.text:
Weighted average of the fired singletons gives the normalized step, scaled by the maximum step \(\Delta D_\text{max}\):

\[\Delta D = \Delta D_\text{max}\, \frac{\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}\, r_{ij}}{\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}}, \qquad D_{k+1} = \operatorname{clip}(D_k + \Delta D).\]

Singleton outputs (Sugeno-style defuzzification) keep the controller cheap: no output-set integration. This matters for the MCU port.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: mpp_sdk.FuzzyLogic(initial_duty, e_scale, de_scale, max_step, …). The scales \(s_E, s_{\Delta E}\) tune aggressiveness and depend on the panel's current/voltage ranges. On the first call there is no previous sample, so the controller records \((V, P)\) and perturbs by one full \(\Delta D_\text{max}\) step (not graduated), same as P&O's priming step.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Subudhi, B., & Pradhan, R. (2013). A comparative study on maximum power point tracking techniques for photovoltaic power systems. IEEE Transactions on Sustainable Energy.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: Incremental Conductance tracks the MPP by comparing the panel's incremental conductance \(\Delta I/\Delta V\) against its instantaneous conductance \(-I/V\). At the maximum power point the two are equal, which gives an explicit "at-the-MPP" test that P&O lacks.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The maximum of \(P = V\cdot I\) occurs where \(dP/dV = 0\). Expanding,

\[\frac{dP}{dV} = \frac{d(VI)}{dV} = I + V\frac{dI}{dV} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{dI}{dV} = -\frac{I}{V}.\]

This yields the three-way decision:

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta V} &> -\frac{I}{V} &&\Rightarrow\; \text{left of MPP, raise } V,\\ \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta V} &= -\frac{I}{V} &&\Rightarrow\; \text{at MPP, hold},\\ \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta V} &< -\frac{I}{V} &&\Rightarrow\; \text{right of MPP, lower } V. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Division-free form
docs.text:
To avoid dividing by \(\Delta V\) (which is zero when the operating point is steady), multiply through by \(V\,\Delta V\) and compare signs:

\[\operatorname{sign}\!\big(\Delta I\, V + I\, \Delta V\big) \quad\text{against}\quad \operatorname{sign}(\Delta V).\]

When they agree, the operating point is left of the MPP.

The special case \(\Delta V \approx 0\) (division would blow up) falls back to the sign of \(\Delta I\): rising current (\(\Delta I > 0\)) is read as left of the MPP (raise \(V\)), falling current (\(\Delta I < 0\)) as right of it (lower \(V\)), and \(\Delta I \approx 0\) as at the MPP (hold).

On the first call there is no previous sample, so the controller records \((V, I)\) as the reference and perturbs by one step, same as P&O.

docs.title: SEPIC sign convention
docs.text: Same as P&O: \(R_\text{eff}(D)=R_\text{load}\left(\tfrac{1-D}{D}\right)^2\) is decreasing in \(D\), so "raise \(V\)" maps to "decrease \(D\)". InCond is a drop-in replacement for P&O.

docs.title: Advantages and limits
docs.text:
• vs. P&O: the explicit MPP condition lets it hold still at the peak, reducing steady-state oscillation, and it responds more cleanly to fast irradiance changes.
  • Partial shading: still a local, gradient-following method. It is trapped on local maxima just like P&O.

docs.text: mpp_sdk.IncrementalConductance(initial_duty, step_size, min_duty, max_duty).

docs.title: References
docs.text: Hussein et al. (1995), Maximum photovoltaic power tracking: an algorithm for rapidly changing atmospheric conditions, IEE Proc.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: Particle Swarm Optimization is a population-based global search. A swarm of candidate duty cycles ("particles") explores the operating range, each one pulled toward its own best-seen point and the swarm's best-seen point. Because the search is global, it finds the global MPP on a multi-modal (partially shaded) P-V curve, where gradient methods get trapped.

docs.title: Particles
docs.text:
Particle \(i\) has a position \(x_i\) (a duty cycle), a velocity \(v_i\), and a personal-best position \(p_i\) (the duty that gave it the most power so far). The swarm shares the global-best position \(g\) (best duty any particle has found). The fitness of a position is the measured power \(P = V\cdot I\) at that duty.

Particles are initialised spread evenly across \([D_\text{min}, D_\text{max}]\), so the first pass doubles as a coarse scan that brackets the global peak's basin.

docs.title: Sequential evaluation
docs.text: The rig can only test one duty at a time (one panel, one converter), so particles are evaluated one per control step. A full PSO iteration takes \(n_\text{particles}\) control steps: command each particle's duty, read its power on the next step, then update \(p_i\) and \(g\).

docs.title: Update rule
docs.text:
After every particle in an iteration has been evaluated, positions and velocities are updated with the canonical PSO equations:

\[v_i \leftarrow w\,v_i + c_1 r_1\,(p_i - x_i) + c_2 r_2\,(g - x_i),$$ $$x_i \leftarrow \operatorname{clip}\big(x_i + v_i,\; D_\text{min},\, D_\text{max}\big),\]

where \(r_1, r_2 \sim U(0,1)\) and:

  • \(w\) (inertia): how much previous velocity is retained (exploration).
  • \(c_1\) (cognitive) weight: pull toward the particle's own best.
  • \(c_2\) (social) weight: pull toward the swarm's global best.

Over successive iterations the particles contract around \(g\), which converges to the global MPP.

docs.title: Convergence and hand-off
docs.text: After \(M\) iterations (cost \(\approx M\cdot n_\text{particles}\) steps) the swarm has converged. Control is handed to a local PerturbAndObserve seeded at \(g\), which refines the operating point and keeps steady-state oscillation low. PSO alone would keep jittering as particles never fully stop.

docs.title: Restart on shading change
docs.text:
Once handed off, the controller is a plain P&O and cannot escape a local maximum when the shading pattern changes. The same two triggers as ScanAndTrack re-run the search: a PowerChangeDetector watching \(P = V\,I\) during tracking (on by default), and an optional periodic rescan_period backstop. See restart_policy.md for how each one works and for the derivation behind the deployed period.

What a PSO restart does is specific to the swarm: it re-seeds every particle evenly across the duty range and discards the personal and global bests, so the next search starts clean instead of reusing bests from the shading condition that no longer holds.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• Swarm size / iterations: larger ⇒ more reliable global capture but a longer, lossier search before lock-on.
  • vs. scan-and-track: PSO can need fewer evaluations than a fine full scan on wide ranges, but it is stochastic (seed-dependent) and can still miss a very narrow peak with too few particles. Scan-and-track is deterministic.
  • MCU cost: state is \(\sim 4\,n_\text{particles}\) floats, small for modest swarms; the RNG and per-iteration update are cheap.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
mpp_sdk.ParticleSwarm(initial_duty, n_particles, inertia, cognitive, social, max_iterations, track_step, min_duty, max_duty, seed, restart_threshold, restart_samples, rescan_period). A fixed seed makes runs reproducible, as required by the project's reproducibility policy.

Swarm size matters more than it looks on a real (or dynamic-simulated) rig. Each particle's fitness is measured one control period after commanding it, while the input capacitor is still slewing, so the first (coarse-scan) iteration sees lag-corrupted powers. On the 2-panel Hissuma rig at a 1 kHz loop, 6 particles locate the global basin for only ~60 % of seeds after a shading change. 8 particles are reliable.

Because the swarm's convergence depends on the RNG stream, stochastic algorithms are reported as mean +/- std over 30 seeds, never a single seed (harness/compare_seeds.py). See restart_policy.md for the measured eta and trap counts and how they compare against ScanAndTrack.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Kennedy & Eberhart (1995), Particle swarm optimization, ICNN. Miyatake et al. (2011), MPPT of multiple PV arrays: a PSO approach, IEEE TAES. Liu et al. (2012), A PSO-based MPPT for PV under partial shading, IEEE TEC. Dolara et al. (2018), An Evolutionary-Based MPPT Algorithm for Photovoltaic Systems under Dynamic Partial Shading, Applied Sciences.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: Perturb & Observe is the canonical hill-climbing MPPT method. It periodically perturbs the converter duty cycle \(D\) by a fixed step and observes the resulting change in panel power \(P = V\cdot I\). If power increased, it keeps moving in the same direction; if power dropped, it reverses.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The panel power-voltage curve \(P(V)\) is unimodal (single peak) under uniform irradiance, with a single maximum where

\[\frac{dP}{dV} = 0.\]

P&O estimates the sign of \(dP/dV\) from successive samples:

\[\Delta P = P_k - P_{k-1}, \qquad \Delta V = V_k - V_{k-1}.\]

The decision rule (in terms of the voltage the algorithm should move toward):

\(\Delta P\) \(\Delta V\) Action \(> 0\) \(> 0\) keep raising \(V\) \(> 0\) \(< 0\) keep lowering \(V\) \(< 0\) \(> 0\) lower \(V\) \(< 0\) \(< 0\) raise \(V\) \(= 0\) any hold

For the four non-zero rows, the desired voltage move has the sign of \(\Delta P \cdot \Delta V\). The implementation does not compute that product directly: it holds only when \(\Delta P = 0\), and otherwise raises \(V\) unless \(\Delta P \cdot \Delta V > 0\). So the edge case \(\Delta V \approx 0\) with \(\Delta P \neq 0\) (duty already saturated at a bound, so the last perturbation did not move \(V\)) falls into the "raise \(V\)" branch rather than holding. This is harmless in practice: it only arises while \(D\) is clamped, where the move is a no-op anyway.

On the very first call there is no previous sample to compare against, so the controller just records \((V, P)\) as the reference and perturbs by one \(+\Delta D\) step, picking an arbitrary starting direction.

docs.title: SEPIC sign convention
docs.text:
For the SEPIC stage, the reflected input resistance is

\[R_\text{eff}(D) = R_\text{load}\left(\frac{1-D}{D}\right)^2,\]

which is monotonically decreasing in \(D\). So raising \(D\) lowers the panel voltage. The voltage decision is therefore mapped to its inverse in duty: to raise \(V\), decrease \(D\); to lower \(V\), increase \(D\). Written against the table above,

\[D_{k+1} = D_k - \operatorname{sign}(\Delta P\,\Delta V)\,\Delta D \quad\text{when } \Delta V \neq 0,\]

with the \(\Delta V \approx 0\), \(\Delta P \neq 0\) edge case handled as described above.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• Step size \(\Delta D\): large \(\Rightarrow\) fast convergence but large steady-state oscillation around the MPP; small \(\Rightarrow\) low ripple but slow tracking. This accuracy/speed tension is the method's defining limit.
  • Partial shading: P&O only follows the local gradient, so on a multi-peak curve it gets trapped on a local maximum. Escaping it requires a global method (scan, PSO).

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: mpp_sdk.PerturbAndObserve(initial_duty, step_size, min_duty, max_duty). Fixed step, minimal state (last \(V\), last \(P\)), a few branches, no loops. Ideal for an MCU.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Femia et al. (2005), Optimization of perturb and observe MPPT, IEEE TPEL. Ahmed & Salam (2015), An Improved Method to Predict the Position of Maximum Power Point During Partial Shading for PV Arrays, IEEE TII.

docs.title: Why a trigger policy
docs.text: A global search (ScanAndTrack's full duty sweep, or a PSO pass) physically drives the converter across its range: exploration costs energy, so it cannot run continuously. After the search hands off, the controller is a plain local tracker (PerturbAndObserve) and cannot escape a local maximum once the shading pattern changes again. The open question is when to search again - it moves the results more than the choice of search itself. Two mechanisms, both on the controller side and both fed only by \((V, I)\), answer it: a step detector and a periodic backstop.

docs.title: Step detector
docs.text:
PowerChangeDetector (mpp_sdk/algorithms/restart.py) watches \(P = V\,I\) during tracking and restarts the global search when the power has deviated from its reference by more than threshold (relative, default 20 %) for samples consecutive steps (default 3) - the classic \(|\Delta P|/P\) restart condition used by PSO-MPPT schemes [Liu et al. 2012].

  • Arming after reset: after a reset (construction, or right after a search hands off) the detector follows the raw samples until samples consecutive readings agree within the band, then arms. This makes it immune to the electrical settling transient after the jump to a newly-found peak, with no plant-specific hold-off constant needed.
  • In-band reference follow: once armed, the reference follows the power only while it stays inside the band (an EMA; smoothing=1.0 by default pins it to the last in-band sample). The converter's own continuous transients and slow irradiance ramps - which the local tracker follows on its own - never trigger a restart.
  • Step detector, blind to ramps: a change that creeps in over many control periods is followed, not flagged. An abrupt shading change is a discontinuity and fires within samples steps.
  • State is three scalars (_ref, _count, _armed), plus three fixed configuration values (threshold/samples/smoothing), and the update is branch-light - MCU-portable by design. See the docstring at mpp_sdk/algorithms/restart.py:9-55 for the authoritative behavior; this page is explanatory.

docs.title: Periodic backstop
docs.text:
The detector has one blind spot: a new, higher peak appearing elsewhere while the tracked power barely moves (e.g. shade swapping from one panel to another in a series string). The rescan_period backstop covers it by re-running the search every \(M\) control steps unconditionally:

\[\text{if } (\text{steps since last scan}) \ge M \;\Rightarrow\; \text{restart the search.}\]

It bounds the worst-case trapped time to one period, at the price of one search's energy cost per period.

docs.title: Choosing the period: expected-loss model
docs.text:
harness/compare_rescan.py sweeps rescan_period over {250, 500, 1000, 2000, off} for the global trackers on the cyclic schedule and derives the optimum from first principles, then checks it against the measurement. The loss, as a fraction of available energy, is modelled as

\[L(P) = \frac{A}{P} + B \cdot P,\]

where the first term is the search tax and the second is trap exposure:

  • \(A\) (search tax): a periodic re-search costs a fixed energy \(e_s\). This is measured in a steady-full-sun calibration run where re-scanning is the only loss (backstop off vs. backstop on every CAL_PERIOD steps, same unchanging condition): the extra energy lost, divided by the re-search count, gives \(e_s\). Over \(N\) schedule steps there are about \(N/P\) periodic re-searches, so \(A = e_s \cdot N / E_\text{available}\).
  • \(B\) (trap exposure): with the backstop off, stealth traps cost a fraction \(L_\text{off}\) of the available energy (measured on the same backstop-off run used for the calibration above). A trap persists until the next periodic re-search, on average \(P/2\); for periods below the mean plateau length \(D\) the exposure scales with \(P\), so \(B = L_\text{off} / D\).

Minimising \(L(P)\) gives the derived optimum

\[P^\star = \sqrt{A / B} \approx 1035 \text{ control steps},\]

which lands on the empirical best: Scan&Track's eta energy peaks at 95.0 % at period 1000 (the nearest swept value to \(P^\star\)). Over-frequent re-scanning (period 250) actually traps more often, not less. Each sweep is itself a window during which a mid-scan shading change can go undetected, so shortening the period below the plateau timescale adds risk instead of removing it. harness/compare_rescan.py regenerates this table and the accompanying figure (harness/output/compare_rescan.png).

docs.title: Measured behavior
docs.text:
Local trackers (no restart policy) trap in roughly half the shaded plateaus of the cyclic schedule, settling at 44-66 % of available power on those traps (docs/methodology.md). The configured global trackers (rescan_period=1000, detector on) cut traps to a handful at the price of up to ~1 s re-acquisition when only the backstop can free them.

Stochastic search is measured the same way, over seeds rather than periods: harness/compare_seeds.py runs PSO (8 particles, rescan_period=1000) over 30 seeds on the cyclic schedule and reports eta 93.9 % +/- 0.7 and 7.9 +/- 1.7 trapped plateaus, against the deterministic Scan&Track at 95.0 % eta and 5 traps with zero variance. Scan&Track beats PSO's mean on both metrics and removes seed-to-seed variance entirely. That is why it is the MCU deployment candidate - see scan_and_track.md and particle_swarm.md for the per-algorithm detail.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Liu et al. (2012), A PSO-based MPPT for PV under partial shading, IEEE TEC.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: Under partial shading the P-V curve becomes multi-modal: bypass diodes create several local maxima, only one of which is the global MPP. Gradient followers (P&O, InCond, fuzzy) climb the nearest peak and get trapped on a local maximum. Scan-and-track avoids this in two stages: first scan the whole operating range to locate the global peak, then track it locally for low-ripple steady state.

docs.title: Stage 1: Scan
docs.text:
Sweep the duty cycle across its full range in fixed increments and record the power at each point:

\[D_k = D_\text{min} + k\,\Delta D_\text{scan}, \qquad k = 0,1,\dots,N, \qquad N = \left\lceil \frac{D_\text{max}-D_\text{min}}{\Delta D_\text{scan}} \right\rceil.\]

Because raising \(D\) lowers the panel voltage on a SEPIC (\(R_\text{eff}(D)=R_\text{load}\left(\tfrac{1-D}{D}\right)^2\)), sweeping \(D\) sweeps the entire P-V curve, so every local peak, including the global one, is sampled. The global-best duty is

\[D^\star = D_{\,\arg\max_k P(D_k)}.\]

The scan costs \(N{+}1\) control steps of swept (sub-optimal) power before locking on. This is the price paid to guarantee the global peak rather than a local one. A measurement at step \(k\) corresponds to the duty commanded at step \(k{-}1\), so powers are recorded with one step of latency.

docs.title: Stage 2: Track
docs.text: Jump to \(D^\star\) and hand off to a local tracker (here PerturbAndObserve) with a small step \(\Delta D_\text{track}\ll\Delta D_\text{scan}\). This refines the operating point onto the exact peak and keeps steady-state oscillation low.

docs.title: Re-scanning
docs.text: The shading pattern changes over the day, moving the global peak. Without a re-acquisition mechanism the controller is a plain P&O after the first scan and stays trapped on whatever peak the change leaves it on. Two mechanisms restart Stage 1: a PowerChangeDetector watching \(P = V\,I\) during Stage 2 (on by default), and an unconditional periodic re-scan every rescan_period steps (off by default). Both are shared with ParticleSwarm; see restart_policy.md for how each one works, and for the derivation behind the deployed rescan_period.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• \(\Delta D_\text{scan}\): finer ⇒ won't miss a narrow global peak, but a longer (lossier) scan.
  • vs. local methods: the only one of the four that reaches the global MPP under partial shading; in full sun it matches them but pays the one-time scan cost at startup.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: mpp_sdk.ScanAndTrack(initial_duty, scan_step, track_step, min_duty, max_duty, rescan_period, restart_threshold, restart_samples). State is one power array of length \(N{+}1\) plus the embedded P&O and the four-scalar restart detector, small and bounded, suitable for the MCU port.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Patel & Agarwal (2008), MPPT scheme for PV systems operating under partially shaded conditions, IEEE TIE. Dolara et al. (2016), A novel MPPT algorithm for photovoltaic systems under dynamic partial shading: Recurrent scan and track method, IEEE ICRERA.

docs.title: Bench Session Metrics: Two Panels, 50 Ohm
docs.text:
This document evaluates the 15 closed-loop hardware runs from data/bench/two_panels_50R_20261017/ (commit 15d427f), retaining only the core metrics selected for the project's comparison benchmark (as formalized in metrics_summary.md and metrics_analysis.md).

Redundant metrics (static \(\eta\), raw power ripple \(\Delta P_{pp}\), non-physical overshoot \(OS\), \(MAE\), \(RE\)) have been omitted in favor of normalized, physically discriminative indicators.

docs.title: 1. Selected Core Metrics Applied
docs.text: Metric Symbol Definition / Setting Role in Comparison Steady-State Efficiency \(\eta_{ss}\) Mean of \(P\) over the tail of the run divided by \(P_{mpp}\). The SDK function final_efficiency averages the last last_n samples (default 100); the table below used the final 30 % of the samples. Checks convergence quality after search transients extinguish. Local Trap Depth \(D_{trap}\) \(\frac{P_{settled}}{P_{global\_mpp}}\) (equivalent to \(\eta_{ss}\) on multi-peak curves). Decisive under partial shading: quantifies power lost when stuck on a secondary peak. Settling Time \(T_c\) First sample after which the entire trace stays at or above 95 % of \(P_{mpp}\) (one-sided band, as in settling_time). Reported in seconds and steps. Measures initial acquisition speed. Step count provides the invariant bridge to simulation (\(1\text{ ms}\) vs \(\sim 46\text{ ms}\)). Transient Energy Loss \(E_{loss}\) \(\int_0^{T_c} (P_{mpp} - P(t))\,dt\) [Joules], trapezoid rule on the sample times. Exact energy cost burned during the convergence search. Differentiates algorithms that reach the same \(\eta_{ss}\). Normalized RMSE \(nRMSE\) \(\frac{1}{P_{mpp}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{tail}(P_k - P_{mpp})^2} \times 100\%\) Penalizes tail oscillations quadratically; normalized across different light levels. Panel Voltage Ripple \(\Delta V_{pp}\) \(\max(V_{tail}) - \min(V_{tail})\) [Volts]. Measures electrical stress and input bus voltage oscillation induced by duty dithering.
