docs.text:
1. Trap Depth (\(D_{trap}\)) vs. Error (\(nRMSE\)):
  2. On the global peak, \(nRMSE \approx 0.5\text{–}0.6\%\), reflecting clean tracking.
  3. On the local trap, \(nRMSE\) jumps to \(11\text{–}13\%\), directly reflecting the \(12\%\) power deficit.
  4. Transient Cost (\(E_{loss}\)) vs Settling Time (\(T_c\)):
  5. \(E_{loss}\) in Joules provides a direct physical penalty. Fuzzy settled at 100% \(\eta_{ss}\) in Scenario 1, but its sluggish response cost 12.54 J.
  6. Reporting \(T_c\) in steps (e.g. 21 to 44 steps) normalizes hardware execution against the \(1\text{ ms}\) simulation model.
  7. Scan&Track Dominance under Static Shading:
  8. Scan&Track is the only algorithm that reached the global peak autonomously without operator bias in initial duty. Its scan cost \(2.39\text{ J}\) and 24 steps, easily offset by avoiding the \(12\%\) local trap.

docs.title: ADC calibration (hardware v1)
docs.text: The board measures V in with the INA229, and V out with the RP2040's on-chip ADC. The INA229 needs no calibration. The on-chip ADC does, and this page explains why and how.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• The ADC gives a raw code (0 to 4095). The firmware converts it with one straight line, then multiplies by the divider ratio (8.5 on Low):
pin voltage = 0.79322 mV x (code - 13.19)
  • The gain (0.79322 mV per code) and the zero (13.19 codes) are in firmware/pipico_board/src/adc_cal.rs. ADC_PWR, ADC_VOUT and ADC_Input_Curr share one ADC, so they share the line.
  • The ADC reads about 13 codes at 0 V. On Low that is about 90 mV at the terminals. Before the calibration, V out showed 85-95 mV with 0 V on the output, and readings below 1.2 V were 6-16 % high. From 3 V to 18 V they were within 0.5 %.

Check against a multimeter (2026-09-19):

Test Meter ADC_VOUT Output at 0 V, converter off 0.000 V 0.000 V Supply on the output 5.030 V 5.006 V Converter switching, D = 0.45, 5 V in, 10 Ohm load 3.2 V 3.221 V Converter switching, D = 0.40, 12 V in, 10 Ohm load 7.00 V 7.006 V

Remaining error

The RP2040 ADC has uneven code steps near codes 512 and 1536 (errata RP2040-E11; about 3.4 V and 10.2 V at the terminals on Low). A straight line cannot follow them: expect up to about 50 mV of error there. For better accuracy, use the INA229 (V in only).

docs.title: When to redo it
docs.text:
• On a different board, or after you change the Pico.

Changing the ADC range does not need a redo. The gain and zero describe the RP2040's own ADC, not the divider ahead of it. See "Changing the ADC range" below for what a range change does need.

docs.title: How to redo it (about 15 minutes)
docs.text:
You need a bench power supply and a multimeter.

  1. Keep the duty at 0. Leave the workbench server idle. Do not press Start Measurement or Start run.
  2. Connect the supply to the input, J3: + on pin 1 or 2, − on pin 3 or
  3. Set the current limit to 50 mA.

  4. Read the log with the debug probe (cargo run --release in firmware/pipico_board). Once per second the firmware prints a line like this:

    ADC cal: PWR raw=1495.4 ... | INA229 V=9970 mV

    raw is the ADC code, and INA229 V is the true voltage.

  5. Take two points, far apart. One low (1-2 V) and one near the top of the range (18 V on Low). Hold each voltage for 10 s and write down raw and INA229 V. Do not use two high points: the zero then comes out wrong.

  6. Calculate the two numbers. With points (c1, V1) and (c2, V2), in codes and terminal mV, and the divider ratio R (8.5 on Low):

    slope = (V2 - V1) / (c2 - c1)       terminal mV per code
zero  = c1 - V1 / slope             codes
gain  = slope / R                   pin mV per code

    Example (2026-09-19): (192.4, 1200) and (2677.6, 17970) give slope 6.748, zero 14.6 and gain 0.7939. The numbers in the firmware come from a fit through all eight points taken that day; two points give almost the same line.

  7. Put them in adc_cal.rs: UV_X100_PER_CODE is the gain in microvolts x 100 (0.7939 mV becomes 79390), ZERO_CODE_X100 is the zero x 100 (14.6 becomes 1460). Build and flash.

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text:
Put the supply on the output, J4: + on pin 1 or 2, − on pin 3 or 4. This is safe with the duty at 0: the output diode stops the supply from feeding the converter. Compare ADC_VOUT in the log against the meter at two or three voltages. It must agree within about 50 mV.

Never run the converter with no load

With nothing on the output, the SEPIC output rises far above the input: about 50 V at 10 % duty with 18 V in. To check V out while the converter switches, put a load resistor on the output (10 Ohm, 10 W) and use scripts/duty_sweep.py.

docs.title: Changing the ADC range
docs.text:
The board has three ranges: Low, Mid, Full. Each range trades full-scale voltage for ADC resolution. Low gives the most resolution but the lowest ceiling; Full gives the highest ceiling but the least resolution per volt.

The full-scale values (Low about 27.3 V, Mid about 51.5 V, Full about 75.6 V) are in the range table in firmware/pipico_board/README.md. Use Low for one panel (the firmware default) and Mid for two panels in series (about 35 V open-circuit).

This needs four steps: move the jumpers, set the constant, reflash, and check the result against a meter. It does not need a new gain/zero fit (see "When to redo it" above).

docs.title: 1. Move the jumpers
docs.text:
Both the input divider (feeds ADC_PWR) and the output divider (feeds ADC_VOUT) have three 75k resistors in series ahead of a 10k leg. Two of the three resistors, on each divider, can be bridged out with a jumper:

  • Input: JP6 bridges out one 75k resistor, JP7 bridges out another. JP9 is a fixed link between the input terminal and the rest of the divider. Leave JP9 shorted; it is not part of the range choice.
  • Output: JP8 bridges out one 75k resistor, JP13 bridges out another. JP10 is the equivalent fixed link on the output side. Leave JP10 shorted too.

With no jumper fitted, a divider is in its Full range: that is how the board is built. These designators come from the "AnalogConverters" sheet of the schematic under hardware/.

Short 0, 1, or 2 of {JP6, JP7} (input) and the same count of {JP8, JP13} (output) to pick the range:

Range Input jumpers shorted Output jumpers shorted Full none none Mid one of JP6/JP7 (either) one of JP8/JP13 (either) Low both JP6 and JP7 both JP8 and JP13

The two resistors on each side are the same value (75k, 1%), so it does not matter which one you bridge for Mid.

docs.title: 2. Set the constant
docs.text: In firmware/pipico_board/src/main.rs, set ADC_DIVIDER_RANGE to match the jumpers you just set. This is not auto-sensed. The firmware logs the selected range once at boot as a cross-check.

docs.title: 3. Reflash
docs.text: Build and flash (cargo run --release in firmware/pipico_board, see its README).

docs.title: 4. Check the result
docs.text:
Put a supply on the input, about 2 V, and read the ADC cal: log line against a meter. Then move the supply near the top of the new range (for example, about 25 V on Low) and check again. Expect agreement within about 1 %.

If it is off by more than that, the range's divider ratio is slightly off (the 75k/10k resistors are 1% parts, and three of them stack). Adjust that range's ratio in firmware/pipico_board/src/adc_cal.rs (RATIO_LOW_X100/RATIO_MID_X100/RATIO_FULL_X100) to the measured value. Do not touch the gain or zero: those describe the RP2040's ADC, not the divider, and a range change does not affect them.

docs.title: Input resistance against the ideal SEPIC formula
docs.text:
Check with uv run python scripts/check_rin_model.py. It uses the committed 10 Ohm duty sweep (5 V in, D 0.05 to 0.45) and the two long holds. Measured R_in is V_in / I_in. SEPICConverter is lossless, so it gives the same numbers as the ideal formula R_load * ((1 - D) / D)^2.

  • Median relative error is 5.2 %. The maximum is 409 % (at D 0.05).
  • The ideal formula is within 10 % from D 0.25 to 0.45 (errors 5.2 % at 0.25, 1.2 % at 0.30, -0.9 % at 0.35, -2.5 % to 7.8 % at 0.40, -3.3 % at 0.45).
  • Below D 0.25 the formula is too high: 13 % at D 0.20, 35 % at 0.15, 94 % at 0.10, 409 % at 0.05. The measured R_in is lower because the converter draws more input current than the lossless ratio gives.
  • Fixed losses dominate at low duty. Efficiency (V_out^2 / R_load over V_in * I_in) is 28 % at D 0.05 (35 mW in, 9.9 mW out), 43 % at 0.10, 64 % at 0.20 and 82 % at 0.45. The loss is 25 to 35 mW at D 0.05 to 0.10. A lossless converter would give 2529 Ohm at D 0.05 against 709 Ohm measured.
  • DCM may add to this at low duty, but it is not proven: the data has no inductor current.
  • I_in is only about 7 mA at D 0.05 (1 mA resolution, about 14 % there). This does not explain the 409 %.
  • load_ohms comes from the typed --load-ohms argument of scripts/duty_sweep.py, not from a measurement.
  • Use the formula for D above about 0.25 on this bench. Below that, do not rely on it.

docs.title: Dimmer bench tests
docs.text:
This is the procedure to test the lamp dimmer chain on the bench, step by step:

Pi --SPI--> Pico --I2C--> dimmer ESP32-C3 --> TRIAC --> lamp

Status: untested on the bench. The procedure and the script were written without hardware. The script was tested only with a fake source. Expect to correct limits and timings after the first run. Write down every difference. The protocol is in dimmer_link.md.

The order is a safety order. Each test adds one hazard. Do not start a test before the one before it passed.

Test What is connected Hazard 0 Pi, Pico, dimmer on a SELV supply. No mains. No lamp. none 1 Same as Test 0, plus a scope or logic analyser on the SELV side. none 2 Mains and a small lamp (25 to 40 W). mains, fire 3 Mains and the full halogen lamp, with the panels. mains, fire, hot panels

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
Read these before every session.

  • Read hardware/dimmer/README.md and the bring-up order in firmware/esp32c3-dimmer/README.md.
  • The board switches lethal mains voltage. It is an uncertified prototype.
  • Never touch the board, the lamp terminals or a probe while the mains is connected.
  • Do not clip an earthed scope onto the mains side. Probe the SELV side only.
  • A second person is present in Tests 2 and 3. That person can reach the plug.
  • Have a way to cut the mains at once: a plug you can pull, or a switch on a multi-socket.
  • Mains tests: put the mains side behind an isolation transformer or a GFCI, with a fuse in line.
  • Never leave a lamp on and walk away. Never leave a lamp on while you read the screen.
  • Use a small lamp first. Do not use the full halogen lamp before Test 2 passed.
  • If a check leaves the lamp on, or you do not know the lamp state: cut the mains first. Think after.
  • If the exposure limiter trips: the dimmer already switched the lamp off. Do not try to force it on. Send OFF, wait for the cool-down (about 60 s), then continue.
  • If you smell something, see smoke, or see the fuse blow: cut the mains, wait, check by eye and do not power the board again before you know the cause.
  • The script always sends OFF at the end, on an error, on Ctrl-C and on SIGTERM. Do not trust this alone. Watch the lamp.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
• scripts/dimmer_bench.py runs the checks the Pi can see over SPI. --help lists the options.
  • scripts/dimmer_set.py sets or reads the dimmer by hand.
  • A session checklist: create a session from the template dimmer-bench in the workbench.
  • Flash the Pico and the dimmer from the same commit. An old and a new version fail the CRC and the link reads as down.
uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_bench.py --list
uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_bench.py --out results.json            # all Test 0 checks
uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_bench.py --auto-only                   # no human steps
uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_bench.py --only trip --only no-restart

How the script reads results:

  • Each check prints PASS, FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE.
  • The exit code is 0 (all passed), 1 (a check failed), 2 (inconclusive, none failed), 3 (refused to start) or 130 (interrupted).
  • Without --mains the script refuses to command an angle when the status says mains is true. This protects you from a wrong belief that the lamp is disconnected.
  • The script starts a second Python process to hold an angle. It kills that process to test the timeouts.
  • The child process shares the SPI bus with the script. A status read of the script can be split by a keepalive frame of the child. The script then retries the read.
  • The child applies the same mains rule as the script and refuses to start without the mains state of its parent.
  • If the script is killed with SIGKILL while the child holds an angle, the child keeps the angle until its window ends: at most 40 s. Then it sends OFF. Cut the mains if the lamp is lit.
  • no-restart streams on-commands for up to the budget plus 75 s, with no status reads. Only the dimmer trip bounds it (each on-command has a 30 s window, renewed every 10 s). Run it only with no mains (Test 0).
  • --out writes every status read to a JSON file. Keep it with the session.

docs.title: Test 0: Pico to dimmer link, no mains, no lamp
docs.text:
Purpose: test the link, the timeouts and the exposure limiter with no mains. The limiter counts the commanded state, not real firing, so every part works with no mains.

Preconditions:

  • J2 (mains) unplugged. No lamp. J3 empty. JP1 as in the firmware README for the SELV-only case.
  • The dimmer is powered from its own 3.3 V supply. J1 pins 2, 3 and 4 go to the Pico board. Leave pin 1 open on the Pico side (see dimmer_link.md).
  • The Pico and the dimmer run firmware from the same commit. The Pi can reach the Pico over SPI.
  • Optional: a multimeter on FIRE (GPIO4, SELV side). It must stay at 0 V.

Steps and expected readings. Run uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_bench.py --out test0.json, or one check at a time with --only.

Check name What it does Expected reading Pass when link Reads the status 3 s. link_ok true. mains and locked false. All reads valid and as expected. alpha Sets 90 deg, reads back, sets 180 deg, reads back. set_alpha_deg follows. applied_alpha_deg is None. Both read-backs match. stable Polls the status for a minute (--stable-s). link_ok always true. No failed read, status age at most 1.5 s. host-timeout Holds 90 deg in a second process, kills it. set_alpha_deg goes to 180. At 180 within about 4.5 s and stays there. i2c-unplug You unplug the I2C cable on a prompt. link_ok false. False within 4 s of your Enter. Back after you plug it in. spi-unplug You unplug the SPI cable on a prompt. After you plug it back, set angle is 180. Stays 180 over 4 s. deadman You unplug I2C for 4 s on a prompt. timed_out seen after the plug-in. Seen, or INCONCLUSIVE (see below). budget-fall Commands 90 deg, polls 10 s. budget_s falls about 1 per second. Slope 0.8 to 1.2 s per s. budget-rise Lamp off, polls 12 s. budget_s rises about 1 per second. Slope 0.8 to 1.2 s per s. trip Commands on until the trip. tripped after about budget_s seconds. See the limiter steps below. no-restart Streams on-commands past the cool-down. Still tripped and budget_s 0. Then clears after the OFF. reset-clears You reset the dimmer on a prompt. budget_s back to about 120. tripped clear. Both true.

Notes for the timeouts:

  • Pico timeout: the Pico sets alpha to 180 after 3 s without a valid 0xD1. The status comes from a cache up to 1 s old, so the limit in the script is 4.5 s.
  • I2C unplug: the Pico marks the link bad after about 2 s. Your Enter press is the start time, so the measured time has about 1 s of human delay.
  • SPI unplug: the Pi cannot read the Pico while the cable is out. The script kills the holder process, so the Pico sees a stopped host. This cannot tell a lost SPI link from a host timeout. To see the link-loss latch itself, watch the Pico log on its debug port.
  • Dimmer deadman (2 s): the Pico repeats the angle at once after the I2C cable is back, and that clears timed_out. The Pi may never see the flag. Then the result is INCONCLUSIVE. Check the flag on the dimmer USB log (it logs the timeout). Do not count INCONCLUSIVE as a pass.
  • Bad frames: the dimmer counts BAD_FRAMES, but the Pico does not send it to the Pi. The stable check cannot see it. Read it in Test 1 (dimmer USB log or logic analyser).

Limiter steps (the trip and no-restart checks). Total time is about 7 minutes. The lamp is only commanded, never lit, so no mains is needed.

  1. Start with a full budget (wait 2 minutes after earlier checks). The script reads budget_s.
  2. trip: it commands 90 deg in windows of 30 s, renewed every 10 s. It reads the status every second. tripped must be set at about budget_s seconds after the start (120 s from full). The host sends OFF when it sees tripped. That OFF is the acknowledgment.
  3. trip then sends a new on-command. The dimmer must refuse it: tripped stays set.
  4. The OFF came before the cool-down. The dimmer must remember it. tripped must clear at about the trip time plus the budget_s wait that the trip read showed (about 60 s). Not before.
  5. After the clear, a new on-command must be accepted: tripped false and budget_s falls.
  6. no-restart: it streams on-commands for the whole budget, plus the cool-down. It does not read the status (a read that sees tripped makes the host send OFF). Then one read must show tripped set with budget_s 0: cooled and waiting for an OFF. The stream alone must not restart the lamp. After the read the host sends OFF, and tripped must clear within 4 s.
  7. reset-clears: use it when the budget is below 118. Press the EN button on the ESP32-C3 or cycle its power. After about 5 s the link is back, budget_s is about 120 and tripped is clear. Do this with the dimmer log open too.

Write down: the --out JSON file, the measured times (Pico timeout, I2C loss, trip time, re-arm time), the commits of both firmwares, and anything strange (a flickering link_ok, a read that fails).

Fail means: stop, do not go on to mains. Fix the cause first. A FAIL of trip or no-restart means the limiter does not work as designed, so Tests 2 and 3 must wait.

docs.title: Test 1: software I2C master timing on the Pico board
docs.text:
Purpose: the board wires SDA to GPIO5 and SCL to GPIO6. No hardware I2C block of the RP2040 can use that pair, so the Pico firmware drives it in software. Check that the signals fit I2C standard mode (100 kHz).

Preconditions:

  • Test 0 passed. Still no mains and no lamp.
  • A scope or a logic analyser (at least 8 MHz sample rate) on J5 or J8, pins 3 (SDA) and 4 (SCL), ground on pin 2 (GNDA). The 4.7 kohm pull-ups of the Pico board are in place and the cable is short.
  • The dimmer USB log open (log::info! output), to read the bad frame counter.

Steps:

  1. Trigger on a start condition (SDA falls while SCL is high). Capture one status read.
  2. Measure the SCL frequency. Write it down.
  3. Measure these against the I2C standard mode limits: start hold time (4.0 us minimum), stop set-up time (4.0 us minimum), SCL low time (4.7 us minimum), SCL high time (4.0 us minimum).
  4. Measure the SCL and SDA rise time (30 to 70 percent of the supply). With 4.7 kohm and the cable capacitance it must stay below 1000 ns. Check that the logic levels reach 3.3 V.
  5. Decode the frames if the analyser can. Check the address 0x2A, the ACK bits and the CRC bytes.
  6. Poll the status for 10 minutes: uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_set.py --status in a loop, or uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_bench.py --only stable --stable-s 600. Read BAD_FRAMES on the dimmer log before and after.
  7. Old status frame after a skipped read. The dimmer keeps one status frame in its TX buffer. If the master skips a read, the next read gets the old frame. To provoke it:
  8. Run the 1 s status polling from the Pi.
  9. Pause the Pico status reads for a moment (for example stop the Pico log or hold the Pico in a debugger for 1 s), or on the analyser look at two consecutive status reads after a read that was skipped.
  10. Change the alpha (for example 90 deg to 180 deg) and look at how many status reads pass before set_alpha_deg and ALPHA in the status follow.
  11. A lag of one frame (about 0.5 s with the Pico 500 ms status period, 1 s on the Pi side) confirms the old frame. Write down the lag. The lamp is safe either way, because the deadman runs on the dimmer.

Expected readings and pass criteria:

  • SCL frequency: 100 kHz or lower, and stable. Pass when it is not above 100 kHz and the timing limits hold.
  • Start and stop timing: each value is inside the limits above.
  • Rise time: below 1000 ns on both lines.
  • Bad frames: the counter does not rise over 10 minutes. Pass when it stays still. A rising count means a noisy cable or bad timing.
  • Old frame: not a pass or fail test. It is a measurement. Write down whether the lag exists.

Write down: the scope or analyser screenshot (SELV side only, no serial numbers in the picture), the values above, the bad frame count before and after, the lag result.

docs.title: Test 2: mains with a small lamp
docs.text:
Purpose: check the zero-cross lock, the real firing angle range, the lamp power against alpha and that the lamp is dark when it must be.

Preconditions:

  • Tests 0 and 1 passed.
  • A small resistive lamp, 25 to 40 W. Never the full halogen lamp first.
  • The mains side behind an isolation transformer or a GFCI. A fuse in line (see the board design notes for the value). A second person ready to cut the plug. The enclosure is closed, the heatsink and the fuse are fitted.
  • The dimmer has a certified isolated 3.3 V supply on J1 with JP1 fitted, not the laptop USB.
  • Optional: a power meter on the lamp, or a true-RMS meter rated CAT III 300 V across the lamp.
  • If you have no power meter: the panel and the converter on the bench, to capture a curve at each angle.

Steps:

  1. Follow the bring-up order in firmware/esp32c3-dimmer/README.md, step 3, with the lamp on J3. Switch the lamp off in the firmware first (the lamp is off after boot).
  2. Apply the mains. The lamp stays dark.
  3. uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_bench.py --mains --only mains-lock. Type the confirmation line when asked. Expect mains true and locked true. Read the mains frequency from the dimmer log: about 50 Hz.
  4. --mains --only mains-range. It sets 10, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 170 deg, one at a time, each in a short window with OFF between them. Expect applied_alpha_deg equal to the requested angle between about 25 and 153 deg. Outside that range the firmware limits the delay, so the applied angle stops at about 25 or 153 deg. Write down every pair.
  5. Alpha sweep and lamp power. Use short windows (10 s or less) at, for example, 30, 60, 90, 120 and 150 deg: uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_set.py --alpha 90 --hold --max-on-s 10.
  6. With a power meter: write down the power at each angle. Divide by the power at full on. Compare with lamp_power_fraction(alpha) from mpp_sdk.io.dimmer. Use the applied angle, not the requested one.
  7. Without a power meter: use the panel short-circuit current as a light sensor. Capture a curve in the workbench at each angle (one window per curve). Compare Isc against alpha with lamp_power_fraction. Isc rises with light, but not strictly in proportion, so use it only to check the shape and the order.
  8. --mains --only mains-dark. At 180 deg the lamp must be dark. When the holder process is killed, the lamp must be dark within about 4 s. Answer the question about the lamp. You must really look at it.

Expected readings and pass criteria:

  • mains true, locked true, frequency about 50 Hz.
  • Applied angle equal to the requested angle inside about 25 to 153 deg, never outside 24 to 154 deg.
  • Lamp power falls as alpha rises and is near lamp_power_fraction (write down the difference).
  • Lamp dark at 180 deg, and dark after the keepalive stops.
  • No fuse blown, no heat or smell, bad_frames quiet on the dimmer log.

Write down: the pairs requested and applied, the power or Isc at each angle, the frequency, the lamp and the protection used, and the lamp state in the dark checks.

If a check fails, cut the mains first. Do not go on to Test 3.

docs.title: Test 3: full halogen lamp with the panels
docs.text:
Purpose: see the real use: the full lamp lights the panels in short windows. Learn how fast the panels heat and cool, so that the limiter constants can be tuned.

Preconditions:

  • Test 2 passed.
  • The full halogen lamp (about 1 kW) is on J3. The TRIAC heatsink is fitted. The lamp is a heat source: keep it away from anything that burns, with a stand that does not move.
  • The panels sit at the planned distance. A second person watches the lamp and the panels.
  • If you have a temperature probe: on the back of the panel, at the same place every time.
  • The Pi reads the limiter state: budget_s shows on every dimmer_set.py --status line.

Steps:

  1. Record the panel temperature before the first window.
  2. Open a short window (10 s or less): uv run python3 scripts/dimmer_set.py --power 0.5 --hold --max-on-s 10. Capture a curve inside it if the workbench is ready. Never use a window longer than needed.
  3. Record the panel temperature at the end of the window and again 30 s, 60 s and 120 s after the lamp is off. This shows how fast the panels cool when the lamp is off.
  4. Repeat with a longer window (20 s, then 30 s) only if the temperature rise is small. Write down the budget_s before and after each window.
  5. Leave the lamp off for at least 2 minutes between series. The lamp is never on while you wait.

Expected readings and pass criteria:

  • The lamp follows the angle and is off after each window.
  • The panel temperature rise per window is small enough that the next curve is still comparable.
  • budget_s falls during a window and rises after it, as in Test 0.
  • Pass when nothing overheats, the lamp is always off after a window, and the temperature data exist.

Write down: the temperature before and after each window and at 30, 60 and 120 s of cooling, the window lengths and angles, the distance, the room temperature and the budget_s values. The owner uses the data to tune EXPOSURE_MAX_ON_MS and EXPOSURE_RESUME_MS in firmware/dimmer-link/src/lib.rs (see dimmer_link.md).

docs.title: Results table
docs.text:
Copy this table for each session.

Test Check Result Measured value Date Operator Notes 0 link 0 alpha 0 stable 0 host-timeout time to 180 deg: 0 i2c-unplug time to link_ok false: 0 spi-unplug 0 deadman 0 budget-fall / budget-rise rates: 0 trip trip time, re-arm time: 0 no-restart 0 reset-clears 1 SCL frequency kHz: 1 start, stop, rise time 1 bad frames, 10 min before, after: 1 old frame after a skipped read lag: 2 mains and lock Hz: 2 applied angle range 2 lamp power against alpha 2 dark at 180 and after keepalive stop 3 short windows 3 panel temperature and cooling

Use the session template dimmer-bench for the same list in the workbench.

docs.title: What this does not prove
docs.text:
• Nothing here ran on hardware yet. The limits and times in this page are the design values, not measured values.
  • A pass of Test 0 does not prove the lamp is safe on mains. It proves the logic with no mains.
  • The limiter counts commanded on time, not real power or real temperature. It does not tell how hot the panels or the lamp are.
  • The limiter does not cover a stalled dimmer main loop. A stalled loop stops the limiter and the 2 s deadman too. A task watchdog is a later item.
  • The script cannot read the mains frequency or the dimmer BAD_FRAMES: the SPI reply does not carry them.
  • The SPI-unplug check cannot tell a lost SPI link from a host timeout.
  • The power of the lamp against alpha is a model (lamp_power_fraction, resistive lamp). A real lamp is not a pure resistor when cold, and the TRIAC adds leakage at low power.
  • Short windows on a small lamp do not show what a long run with the full lamp does to the panels.
  • One session is one sample. Repeat the checks on another day before you trust the numbers.

docs.title: Dimmer link
docs.text:
The halogen lamp lights the panels. The Pi sets its firing angle alpha through the Pico.

Pi (SPI0 master) --SPI--> Pico (SPI1 slave, I2C master) --I2C--> dimmer ESP32-C3 (I2C slave) --> TRIAC --> lamp
  • The wire format of the I2C side lives in one crate: firmware/dimmer-link. The Pico firmware and the dimmer firmware both use it.
  • The Pi side uses two SPI commands, listed below.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Connect one of the Pico board I2C headers (J5 or J8) to the dimmer connector J1.

Pico board J5 / J8 Net Dimmer J1 Net 1 +3.3V 1 3V3 in 2 GNDA 2 GND 3 I2C_SDA (GPIO5) 3 SDA (ESP32-C3 IO6) 4 I2C_SCL (GPIO6) 4 SCL (ESP32-C3 IO7)
  • The Pico board has 4.7 kohm pull-ups on both lines. The dimmer has none. Keep the cable short.
  • J1 pin 1 powers the ESP32-C3. The dimmer design asks for a regulated 3.3 V supply of at least 1 A. Power the dimmer from its own supply and leave pin 1 open on the Pico side, unless you checked the spare current of the Pico board 3.3 V rail.
  • Connect the grounds. The dimmer ground is the isolated SELV side. The mains side stays behind the optocouplers.
  • On the RP2040, GPIO5 is only I2C0 SCL and GPIO6 is only I2C1 SDA. No I2C block can drive this pair as SDA and SCL, so the Pico firmware drives the pair in software.

docs.title: I2C frames
docs.text:
• 7-bit address 0x2A, 100 kHz, Pico is master.
  • All values are big-endian. The CRC is CRC-8, polynomial 0x07, init 0xFF, the same as the SPI link.

Command (master writes 4 bytes):

[ CMD | ARG_H | ARG_L | CRC ]
CMD Name ARG 0x01 Set alpha alpha in 0.01 degree. 0 is full on, 18000 is off. Above 18000 is rejected. 0x02 Request status 0

Status (master reads 9 bytes, at least 3 ms after Request status):

[ 0xD1 | FLAGS | ALPHA_H | ALPHA_L | FREQ_H | FREQ_L | BAD_FRAMES | BUDGET_S | CRC ]
  • FLAGS bit 0: mains present. Bit 1: locked to the mains. Bit 2: lamp switched off by the timeout. Bit 3: exposure limit tripped (see Exposure limit).
  • ALPHA is the angle the dimmer really fires at, after its own limits. 0xFFFF means it does not fire.
  • FREQ is the mains frequency in 0.01 Hz. It is 0 without mains.
  • BAD_FRAMES counts rejected commands (wraps). A rising value means a noisy cable.
  • BUDGET_S is the exposure budget in seconds, at most 255. Not tripped: lamp-on time left before a trip. Tripped: seconds until the dimmer has cooled. 0 while tripped means cooled, waiting for an OFF.
  • The CRC covers bytes 0 to 7.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
The bench tests are in dimmer_bench.md.

  • The dimmer is off after boot.
  • The Pico repeats the last Set alpha every 500 ms. The dimmer turns the lamp off after 2 s without a valid Set alpha.
  • The dimmer checks this timeout in its own loop, not in the I2C code, so a stalled I2C driver cannot keep the lamp on. The timeout also releases the full-on state.
  • A new valid Set alpha clears the TIMED_OUT flag and the lamp follows the new angle.
  • The Pi repeats 0xD1 at least every second while the lamp is on. The Pico sets alpha to off after 3 s without a valid 0xD1. A stopped or crashed Pi program switches the lamp off.
  • The Pico sets alpha to off at boot and when the SPI link to the Pi is lost.
  • The dimmer firmware limits the firing delay, so the real range is about 25 to 153 degrees at 50 Hz. The angles 0 (full on) and 18000 (off) are the exceptions. Read ALPHA in the status to see the real value.
  • A lamp that is on for no reason is a fire risk. Keep the lamp under watch while the link is new.

docs.title: Exposure limit
docs.text:
The lamp is open loop, so the dimmer limits how long it may be on. The limit lives on the dimmer, the last part before the mains. It does not depend on the Pico or the Pi. It does not cover a stalled dimmer main loop: that stops the limiter and the deadman too. A task watchdog for this is a later item.

  • The dimmer keeps a "heat" counter in milliseconds. It counts the time the lamp is commanded on, not the time it really fires. So it also runs with no mains, and you can test it on the bench with no mains.
  • The counter rises 1 ms per ms while the lamp is commanded on. It falls 1 ms per ms while the lamp is off, and never goes below 0.
  • At EXPOSURE_MAX_ON_MS (120 s) the dimmer trips. It forces the lamp off at once (in its 10 ms loop) and latches the trip.
  • While tripped, every on-command is refused and the lamp stays off. This holds for I2C and for Wi-Fi.
  • The trip clears only when both are true: the counter is at or below EXPOSURE_RESUME_MS (60 s), and the host sent an explicit OFF after the trip (SetAlpha(18000), or Wi-Fi level 0). An OFF that arrives early is remembered. The deadman and the trip itself do not count as that OFF. So a host that keeps sending its old angle never restarts the lamp by itself. It must send OFF, then ask again.
  • The Pico also sends its own OFF at boot and after its 3 s host timeout. The dimmer counts that as the acknowledgment. So a crashed or idle host acknowledges by itself, and the next on-command works after the cool-down.
  • The time between two loop ticks is counted when a command arrives, so fast on and off toggling does not hide the on time.
  • The long-run duty is at most 50 percent. Short windows (about 10 s) can repeat until the counter is full.
  • The counter is in RAM only. A dimmer reset clears it and the trip. The lamp is off after a reset, so this is safe.
  • Status: flag bit 3 and BUDGET_S. The Pico copies them to the Pi (SPI reply flag bit 4 and byte 7).
  • Only the tripped bit says the lamp is blocked. BUDGET_S can be 0 while the lamp is still allowed (heat between 119.5 s and 120 s).
  • When link_ok is 0, the tripped bit and BUDGET_S are unknown. The Pico sends 0 and 0. The other dimmer flags keep their last values.
  • BUDGET_S stops at 255 s if EXPOSURE_MAX_ON_MS is ever raised above 255 s.

To change the limits after a bench thermal test:

  • Edit EXPOSURE_MAX_ON_MS and EXPOSURE_RESUME_MS in firmware/dimmer-link/src/lib.rs.
  • Keep EXPOSURE_RESUME_MS below EXPOSURE_MAX_ON_MS.
  • Run cargo test in firmware/dimmer-link.
  • Build and flash the dimmer again.
  • Flash the Pico and the dimmer together. An old Pico with a new dimmer (or the reverse) fails the CRC, so the link reads as down.
  • Check the Python side: its window limit mirrors EXPOSURE_MAX_ON_MS.

docs.title: SPI commands (Pi to Pico)
docs.text:
Both use the 12-byte frame of the measurement protocol with the usual CRC.

CMD Name MOSI 0xD1 Set dimmer alpha [ ALPHA_H \| ALPHA_L \| CHECKSUM \| 0xD1 \| 0 x 8 ]. The Pico ignores a value above 18000. 0xD2 Request dimmer status [ 0 \| 0 \| CHECKSUM \| 0xD2 \| 0 x 8 ]

The reply to 0xD2 is in the MISO of the next exchange, like the sweep progress poll:

[ 0xD2 | FLAGS | SET_H | SET_L | APPLIED_H | APPLIED_L | AGE | BUDGET_S | CHECKSUM | ACK | 0x00 x 2 ]
  • FLAGS bit 0: the I2C link works (a status read succeeded in the last second). Bits 1 to 3 are the dimmer flags from above, shifted up by one: bit 1 mains, bit 2 locked, bit 3 timed out, bit 4 tripped.
  • BUDGET_S (byte 7) is the budget from the I2C status. Without a good status read in the last second, BUDGET_S is 0 and the tripped bit is clear. Bit 0 then tells that the data is old.
  • The CRC covers bytes 0 to 7, then ACK (byte 9), then byte 10 (SETTLED, always 0 here), in that order. Every MISO frame does the same.
  • SET is the alpha the Pico holds now. It is the last alpha the Pi sent, or 18000 after a timeout or a link loss. APPLIED is the angle the dimmer reported.
  • AGE is the time since the last good status read, in 100 ms units, saturating at 255.

docs.title: Lamp power
docs.text: For a resistive lamp the power fraction at angle alpha is P = 1 - alpha/pi + sin(2 alpha)/(2 pi).

docs.title: Python use
docs.text:
• SpiMcuSource sends the commands.
  • Every "lamp on" has a deadline: max_on_s (default 60 s, at most 120 s, else ValueError). The lamp is open loop, so a lamp that stays on by mistake is a fire risk.
  • A thread repeats the last alpha every second (the dimmer_keepalive_s argument, at most 2 s). At the deadline the same thread sends OFF and stops, also if the caller hangs.
  • A new set_dimmer_* call starts a new deadline. dimmer_window_left_s() gives the time left (None when the lamp is off).
  • lamp_window(power=...) or lamp_window(alpha_deg=...) is the safe way to use the lamp. It sets the lamp, then waits up to 1.5 s (poll every 0.25 s) for a valid status with link_ok. It always sends OFF when the block ends (3 tries), also on an exception or Ctrl-C. It raises DimmerRefused (after OFF) if the link is not confirmed or the dimmer reports tripped. timed_out is not checked: the Pico reports it from a cache that can be 1 s old.
  • If dimmer_status() shows tripped while the host thinks the lamp is on, it sends OFF. That OFF is the acknowledgment the dimmer needs before it accepts "on" again.
  • tripped and budget_s are unknown when link_ok is false (the Pico sends 0 and 0). budget_s == 0 does not mean blocked: only tripped does. The Pico's own OFF (at boot and after its 3 s host timeout) also counts as the OFF acknowledgment.
  • close() and dimmer_off() stop the thread and switch the lamp off.
  • scripts/dimmer_set.py does the same from the command line. With --hold, --max-on-s sets the longest time the lamp stays on. The status line shows tripped and budget_s.
with SpiMcuSource() as src:
    with src.lamp_window(power=0.5, max_on_s=10.0):
        measure()  # the lamp is on here and off afterwards
    print(src.dimmer_status())

docs.title: MPPT measurement protocol
docs.text: How one closed-loop measurement works, and why it works this way.

docs.title: Why: stale telemetry makes the voltage drift up
docs.text:
Early bench runs of P&O, Incremental Conductance and Fuzzy Logic drifted to voltages above \(V_\text{mpp}\), up to \(V_\text{oc}\). The cause:

  1. The SPI bus is full-duplex. The Pico loads the 12-byte MISO frame into its TX FIFO before the transaction. So the telemetry that comes back with write(D_k) shows the state under \(D_{k-1}\) or earlier.
  2. On a SEPIC, a higher duty \(D\) lowers the panel voltage (\(R_\text{in} = R_\text{load}((1-D)/D)^2\)). A lower \(D\) raises it toward \(V_\text{oc}\).
  3. The algorithm raises \(D\) and reads stale data where the voltage has not dropped yet. It sees the wrong slope \(\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}V\) (or the wrong conductance increment) and flips to lower \(D\). Repeated flips push the voltage up to \(V_\text{oc}\).

The fix is a strict request-response sequence with one settled measurement per duty.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Host as Host/sbc (MPPT Controller)
    participant Pico as RP2040 Pico (SEPIC Controller)
    participant HW as Hardware (SEPIC & Sensors)

    Host->>Pico: 1. Send commanded duty D over SPI
    Note over Pico: Erase all measurement buffers
    Pico->>HW: 2. Apply duty D to PWM gate driver
    Note over Host: 3. Wait reaction delay & erase Host/sbc buffers
    Note over Pico,HW: 4. Wait hardware reaction delay (2 ms)
    loop Settle Detection
        Pico->>HW: 5. Monitor Vin until settled (drift < 40 mV)
    end
    Note over Pico,HW: 6. Capture 25 raw samples of Vin, Vout, I
    Note over Pico: 7. Filter: Drop 4 min & 4 max, average middle 17
    Note over Pico: 8. Hold single measurement (NO continuous streaming)
    Host->>Pico: 9. Ask for measurement (CMD_READ_MEASUREMENT)
    Pico-->>Host: 10. Send the ONE settled measurement (is_settled = 1)
    Note over Pico: Clear settled flag (stops streaming)
    Note over Host: 11. Execute MPPT step on clean values (no host filtering)

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. The Host/sbc sends the duty \(D\) over SPI (write(D)).
  2. The Pico zeroes all measurement registers (MEAS_V_MV, MEAS_I_MA, MEAS_ADC_VOUT_MV, ...), clears DUTY_SETTLED and updates the PWM compare register.
  3. The Host/sbc waits at least \(5 - 10\,\text{ms}\) and flushes its local telemetry cache and SPI input buffers.
  4. The Pico waits \(2\,\text{ms}\) for the SEPIC inductors and coupling capacitors to start the transition.
  5. The Pico watches \(V_\text{in}\) in an 8-sample rolling window until the drift is below \(40\,\text{mV}\) (ceiling \(80\,\text{ms}\)).
  6. The Pico takes 25 consecutive readings of \(V_\text{in}\), \(V_\text{out}\) and \(I\). For each channel it sorts them, drops the 4 lowest and the 4 highest, and averages the middle 17.
  7. The Pico stores the result in MEAS_*, sets DUTY_SETTLED = true and parks. It runs no background sampling and does not overwrite the result with raw 1 ms readings.
  8. The Host/sbc sends _CMD_READ_MEASUREMENT (0x02).
  9. The Pico returns the one settled frame with is_settled = 1 and clears DUTY_SETTLED.
  10. The algorithm uses the values as they are. The host does no filtering or averaging.

Implementation notes:

  • The 2 ms delay is Timer::after_millis(2).await in onchip_adc_task, started by MEAS_TRIGGER_COUNT.
  • The settle check ends by asserting SETTLED_TRIGGER.
  • The filter averages samples[4..21] on the INA229 and ADC channels.
  • sensors_task and onchip_adc_task run only on a trigger in MPPT mode. The raw 1 kHz loop is off.

docs.title: Filter Specification (25-Sample Trimmed Mean)
docs.text:
Let \(S = [s_0, s_1, \dots, s_{24}]\) be an array of 25 consecutive ADC readings for a given channel (\(V_{\text{in}}\), \(V_{\text{out}}\), or \(I\)):

  1. Sort: $\(S_{\text{sorted}} = \text{sort}(S)\)$
  2. Trim Outliers:
  3. Discard \(S_{\text{sorted}}[0 \dots 3]\) (4 lowest)
  4. Discard \(S_{\text{sorted}}[21 \dots 24]\) (4 highest)
  5. Compute Average: $\(\bar{S} = \frac{1}{17} \sum_{k=4}^{20} S_{\text{sorted}}[k]\)$

docs.title: SEPIC settling time
docs.text: Why the step response was slow, what fixed it, and the measured result.

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
• A step on the duty cycle took about 100 ms to settle at a 50 kHz switching frequency. That is about 5000 switching cycles (20 us each).
  • The main cause was the \(1000\,\mu\text{F}\) input capacitor in parallel with the panel. The panel has limited current, so it charges and discharges that capacitor slowly.
  • You cannot remove the input capacitor. Without it the panel sees the raw 50 kHz ripple and the ADC readings are distorted. A value of \(22 - 100\,\mu\text{F}\) is enough for the ripple.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Four changes, in this order:

  1. Smaller capacitor. Replace the \(1000\,\mu\text{F}\) capacitor with a \(22\,\mu\text{F}\) low-ESR part. The RC time constant falls by about 5 times. The worst hardware lag falls from 68.4 ms to about 15 ms.
  2. 20 ms mains notch. The lamps of the solar simulator produce a 100 Hz ripple of \(\pm 30 - 50\,\text{mV}\). A burst of 25 samples over 1.25 ms (50 us spacing) caught a random phase of it. This inverted the \(\Delta V\) slope in fine MPPT steps (0.2 % to 0.5 %) and the voltage drifted toward \(V_\text{oc}\). The firmware now spaces the 25 samples by 800 us (Timer::after_micros(800)). The window is exactly 20 ms: 1 cycle of 50 Hz and 2 cycles of 100 Hz. The sine ripple integrates to zero and the steady-state ripple falls to 0.0 mV pp.
  3. Outlier rejection and flush. The firmware takes a 25-sample trimmed mean (drops the 4 lowest and 4 highest, averages the middle 17). On a duty change command the Pico clears its buffers, waits for the hardware transition, computes the settled value and holds that one measurement. It does not stream raw readings.
  4. Driver and step size.
  5. SpiMcuSource has a raw mode (settling_time_s = 0.0). The step response tool scripts/sepic_step_response.py uses it to record transients every 3 ms.
  6. For closed-loop tracking, settling_time_s is 0.05 (50 ms). This covers the filter and the hardware.
  7. With \(\Delta D = 0.002\) (0.2 %), the algorithms converge to \(V_\text{mpp} \approx 14.30\,\text{V}\) (error under 0.6 % of the sweep peak) with an oscillation span of about 1.0 V.

An adaptive P&O step size is a separate software option. It reduces the number of steps and does not change the settling time of one step.

docs.title: Measured result
docs.text:
Duty steps from 0.40 to 0.70 into a \(10\,\Omega\) load. Settling times in ms:

Duty step \(V_\text{in}\) mean \(V_\text{out}\) \(1000\,\mu\text{F}\), no filter \(22\,\mu\text{F}\), 1.25 ms burst \(22\,\mu\text{F}\) + 20 ms notch 0.40 to 0.45 15.50 V 11.57 to 13.52 V 7.3 14.1 41.1 0.45 to 0.50 13.74 V 13.52 to 14.53 V 23.8 5.5 45.6 0.50 to 0.55 9.58 V 14.53 to 12.15 V 68.4 14.6 42.0 0.55 to 0.60 6.55 V 12.15 to 10.05 V 55.3 14.6 44.5 0.60 to 0.65 4.38 V 10.05 to 8.12 V 41.7 0.0 (artifact) 42.1 0.65 to 0.70 2.87 V 8.12 to 6.44 V 28.2 0.0 (artifact) 42.0
  • The \(V_\text{out}\) and \(V_\text{in}\) ripple is 0.0 mV pp in the last column.
  • The 0.0 ms values are artifacts. The ripple phase hid the transition.
  • The settling time with the notch is uniform: 41.1 to 45.6 ms, mean 42.9 ms. It is the sum of two parts:
  • power stage: about 22.9 ms (L-C-L tank and coupling capacitor, within the \(\pm 2\%\) band, with the \(22\,\mu\text{F}\) capacitor),
  • notch window: 20.0 ms (25 samples x 800 us).
  • \(V_\text{out}\) peaks at 14.53 V (\(P \approx 21.1\,\text{W}\) into \(10\,\Omega\)) at \(D = 0.50\) (\(V_\text{in} \approx 13.74\,\text{V}\)). This matches the panel MPP.

docs.title: Analog divider range: Full or Low
docs.text:
Low (8.5x) gives 2.76 times finer ADC voltage resolution than Full (23.5x). The quantization noise is lower.

Metric Full (235 k / 10 k) Low (85 k / 10 k) Divider ratio 23.5x 8.5x Full scale about 75.6 V about 27.3 V 1 LSB about 23.5 mV about 8.5 mV Ripple, step 0.40 to 0.45 94.0 mV pp (about 4 LSB) 43.0 mV pp (about 5 LSB) Ripple, step 0.45 to 0.50 212.0 mV pp 51.0 mV pp Ripple, step 0.55 to 0.60 517.0 mV pp 77.0 mV pp

For setups with \(V_\text{oc} \le 27.3\,\text{V}\), Low gives the best gradient sensitivity for fine-step MPPT.

For the closed-loop timing diagram and the single-measurement protocol see the measurement protocol.

docs.title: Two-Way ANOVA for Comparing MPPT Algorithms
docs.text: Design document for a planned two-factor analysis of variance for the comparison harness and experimental benchmark. It is not implemented: the repo has no harness/compare_anova.py and no statsmodels dependency yet. The goal is to determine whether the performance differences observed between the five MPPT algorithms are statistically significant, and whether they depend on the operational scenario (algorithm × condition interaction).

docs.title: 1. Why an ANOVA is Needed
docs.text:
A single run per algorithm provides only a point estimate, not a distribution. Without formal statistical testing, we cannot rigorously claim in a paper or thesis that "Algorithm X performs significantly better than Algorithm Y" - only that "under this specific seed and run, X captured more energy than Y".

The two-way ANOVA answers three critical scientific questions:

  1. Main effect A (Algorithm): Is there a statistically significant difference between at least one pair of algorithms, averaged across all test scenarios?
  2. Main effect B (Condition / Scenario): Does the environmental scenario (single peak, partial shading) significantly affect tracking performance?
  3. Interaction A×B (Algorithm × Scenario): Does an algorithm's relative advantage depend on the condition? (e.g. P&O is competitive under uniform full sun but degrades under partial shading - this is a direct interaction effect).

docs.title: 2.1. Factors and Levels
docs.text:
Factor Type Levels Description Factor A - Algorithm Between-subjects 5 levels P&O, InCond, Fuzzy, Scan&Track, PSO Factor B - Scenario Within-subjects / Environmental 2 levels Defined below (§2.2)

Note

The design is a full factorial: every combination of (Algorithm × Scenario) is executed with \(N \ge 5\text{ to }10\) repetitions.

docs.title: 2.2. The Two Planned Benchmark Scenarios (Factor B)
docs.text:
To directly align with the experimental bench campaign, Factor B is defined by the two planned physical scenarios:

Level Scenario Name Physical Setup What It Tests B₁ Uniform Steady (Single Peak) Both panels @ \(90^\circ\), constant lamp power Baseline steady-state efficiency (\(\eta_{ss}\)), lock-on speed (\(T_c\)), and voltage ripple (\(\Delta V_{pp}\)). B₂ Static Partial Shading (Multi-Peak) Panel A @ \(90^\circ\), Panel B @ \(45^\circ\), constant lamp power Susceptibility to local-maximum traps (\(D_{trap}\)), global search capability, and GMPP hit rate (\(HR_{GMPP}\)).

docs.title: 2.3. Dependent Variables
docs.text:
A separate two-way ANOVA can be computed for each primary metric of interest:

Metric Symbol Type Primary Role in ANOVA Steady-State Efficiency \(\eta_{ss}\) Continuous, \([0, 1]\) Primary Headline Metric Normalized RMSE \(nRMSE\) Continuous, \(\ge 0\) Steady-state tracking precision Transient Energy Loss \(E_{loss}\) Continuous, \(\ge 0\) Search transient penalty (Joules) Convergence Time \(T_c\) Continuous, \(\ge 0\) Transient responsiveness

Warning

The GMPP hit rate (\(HR_{GMPP}\)) is a proportion / binary outcome (success/trap). An ANOVA on raw proportions violates normality assumptions. For \(HR_{GMPP}\), use a logistic regression model (generalized linear model with logit link) or Fisher's exact test across algorithms.

docs.title: 2.4. Sources of Repetitions (\(N \ge 5\text{ to }10\))
docs.text:
To satisfy ANOVA variance requirements, each cell must have genuine variability:

Algorithm Class Mechanism for Generating Repetitions Stochastic (PSO) Vary RNG seed: \(\text{seed} \in \{0, 1, \dots, N-1\}\). Local Trackers (P&O, InCond, Fuzzy) Vary starting duty: \(D_0 \in \{0.20, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.50\}\) + natural bench electrical sensor noise. Deterministic Global (Scan&Track) Repeated runs across the physical profile with bench electrical sensor noise and slight lamp thermal drift.

docs.title: 3.1. Assumptions Check
docs.text:
Before running the parametric ANOVA, the planned pipeline would verify:

  1. Normality of Residuals: Shapiro-Wilk test (scipy.stats.shapiro) on model residuals.
  2. Homoscedasticity (Equal Variances): Levene's test (scipy.stats.levene) across groups.

Decision flow:

  • If the Shapiro-Wilk test passes (\(p > 0.05\)) and Levene's test passes: two-way parametric ANOVA, Type II sum of squares.
  • If Shapiro-Wilk passes but Levene's test fails: with a balanced design (\(N \ge 5\) per cell) use a robust two-way ANOVA (the central limit theorem applies). With fewer repetitions, use the non-parametric path.
  • If Shapiro-Wilk fails: non-parametric analysis (Kruskal-Wallis or Aligned Rank Transform).
  • Parametric path with \(p < 0.05\): Tukey HSD pairwise comparisons. Non-parametric path with \(p < 0.05\): Dunn post-hoc test with Bonferroni correction.
  • Otherwise: no statistically significant difference.

docs.title: 3.2. Sketch with statsmodels
docs.text:
statsmodels is not a project dependency yet. The code below is a sketch of the planned analysis.

import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.formula.api import ols
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd

# Two-way ANOVA with Type II Sum of Squares (appropriate for factorial designs)
model = ols("eta ~ C(algorithm) * C(scenario)", data=df).fit()
anova_table = sm.stats.anova_lm(model, typ=2)

# Post-hoc pairwise comparison (Tukey HSD)
tukey = pairwise_tukeyhsd(df["eta"], df["algorithm"], alpha=0.05)

docs.title: 4. Visualisation for Papers & Thesis
docs.text:
The planned analysis would produce:

  1. Interaction Plot: Mean \(\eta\) versus Scenario for each of the 5 algorithms. Non-parallel lines visually demonstrate the Algorithm × Scenario interaction.
  2. Boxplots per Cell: Distribution of \(\eta\) showing spread, median, and outliers across the \(5 \times 2 = 10\) cells.
  3. Tukey HSD Significance Heatmap: Pairwise matrix highlighting which algorithms differ significantly (\(p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001\)).

docs.title: 5. Planned Location and Outputs
docs.text:
Nothing in this section exists in the repo yet. Planned layout:

harness/
├── compare_anova.py          # Main script: processes data & computes ANOVA
├── output/
│   ├── anova_data.csv        # Cleaned dataset (algorithm, scenario, rep, eta, nrmse)
│   ├── anova_table.csv       # Standard ANOVA table (SS, df, MS, F, p-value)
│   ├── anova_interaction.png # Interaction & box plots
│   └── anova_tukey.csv       # Pairwise post-hoc comparisons

docs.text:

  • Yang, B. et al. (2023). State-of-the-art review of MPPT techniques for hybrid PV-TEG systems. Global Energy Interconnection, 6(5), 567–591. (Table 4 uses ANOVA for algorithm benchmarking).

docs.title: Metrics Analysis for Comparing MPPT Algorithms
docs.text: This document details the mathematical justification, experimental feasibility, and practical selection of the metrics used to benchmark MPPT algorithms in the mpp-sdk framework.

docs.title: 1.1. Dynamic Energy Efficiency (\(\eta_E\)) - Implemented (energy_efficiency)
docs.text:
\[\eta_E = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^N P_k \cdot \Delta t_k}{\sum_{k=1}^N P_{mpp}(t_k) \cdot \Delta t_k}\]
  • Role: Energy-weighted efficiency against a time-varying \(P_{mpp}(t)\). Used in cyclic simulation (harness/compare_cyclic.py).

docs.title: 1.2. Steady-State Efficiency (\(\eta_{ss}\)) & Local Trap Depth (\(D_{trap}\)) - Implemented (Selected)
docs.text:
\[\eta_{ss} = \frac{1}{M \cdot P_{mpp}} \sum_{k=N-M+1}^{N} P_k, \qquad D_{trap} = \frac{P_{settled}}{P_{global\_mpp}}\]
  • Code: final_efficiency and trap_depth in mpp_sdk/metrics.py.
  • Role: Evaluates operating point quality once transients extinguish (averaged over the tail of the run: final_efficiency uses the last last_n samples, default 100).
  • Discrimination:
  • On single-peak curves (\(90^\circ\)), all functional algorithms reach \(\eta_{ss} \approx 100\%\).
  • On multi-peak partial-shading curves (\(45^\circ\), Scenario 2), \(D_{trap}\) cleanly separates local trackers trapped on the low-voltage peak (\(D_{trap} \approx 87\text{–}89\%\)) from global trackers reaching the global MPP (\(D_{trap} \approx 100\%\)).

docs.title: 1.3. Convergence Time (\(T_c\)) - Implemented (Selected)
docs.text:
\[T_c = \min \{ t \mid \forall \tau \ge t, \, P(\tau) \ge (1 - \text{band}) P_{mpp} \}\]
  • Code: settling_time in mpp_sdk/metrics.py.
  • Role: Measures tracking speed from cold start.
  • Hardware Units: Must be reported in both seconds and control steps. Because the physical HIL step takes \(\sim 46\text{ ms}\) (due to ADC settling waits and filtering) while simulation runs at \(1\text{ kHz}\) (\(1\text{ ms}\)), step counts provide the true invariant metric between simulation and real hardware.

docs.title: 1.4. Transient Energy Loss (\(E_{loss}\)) - Planned (Selected)
docs.text:
\[E_{loss} = \sum_{k=1}^{T_c} (P_{mpp,k} - P_k) \cdot \Delta t_k\]
  • Role: Quantifies the exact energy penalty (in Joules) incurred during the search transient.
  • Why It Matters: Two algorithms can converge to the same \(\eta_{ss} = 100\%\) and even have similar settling times, but one may stay closer to the peak during the climb while the other wanders or oscillates wildly. In the bench data, Fuzzy and P&O both settled at \(100\%\), but Fuzzy lost \(12.54\text{ J}\) during convergence compared to P&O's \(4.54\text{ J}\).

docs.title: 1.5. Steady-State Normalized RMSE (\(nRMSE\)) - Planned (Selected)
docs.text:
\[RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{k=N-M+1}^{N} (P_k - P_{mpp})^2}, \qquad nRMSE = \frac{RMSE}{P_{mpp}} \times 100\%\]
  • Role: Replaces raw peak-to-peak ripple (\(\Delta P_{pp}\)).
  • Statistical Superiority: Peak-to-peak ripple is easily dominated by single-sample ADC spikes or noise floor (0.07–0.17 W peak-to-peak over the tail in the bench runs). \(nRMSE\) averages deviations over the entire tail, penalizes large excursions quadratically, and normalizes across different power levels.

docs.title: 1.6. GMPP Hit Rate (\(HR_{GMPP}\)) - Planned (Selected)
docs.text:
\[HR_{GMPP} = \frac{N_{success}}{N_{total}} \times 100\%\]
  • Role: Critical for evaluating global MPPT methods (Scan&Track, PSO) under partial shading (Scenario 2).
  • Requirements: Requires repeated runs (\(N \ge 10\)) with varying initial duties \(D_0\) and RNG seeds for PSO.

docs.title: 1.7. Panel Voltage Ripple (\(\Delta V_{pp}\)) - Planned (Selected)
docs.text:
\[\Delta V_{pp} = \max_{k \in \text{tail}} V_k - \min_{k \in \text{tail}} V_k\]
  • Role: Measures electrical stress induced by duty dithering on the SEPIC converter's input bus capacitor.
  • Benchmark Observation: P&O dithering induced \(\sim 1.0\text{–}1.3\text{ V}\) ripple, whereas Fuzzy Logic converged with lower voltage ripple (\(\sim 0.3\text{–}0.8\text{ V}\)).

docs.title: 1.8. Computational Complexity per Cycle (\(t_{step}\)) - Post-Port (Selected)
docs.text:
• Role: Feasibility of MCU deployment on the RP2040.
  • Budget: The target control loop runs at \(1\text{ kHz}\) (\(1000\ \mu s\) total budget).
  • Execution Metric: Execution time per step (\(\mu s\)), RAM usage (out of 264 KB), and Flash footprint (out of 2 MB) measured on the Rust firmware port.

docs.title: 1.9. Simulation vs. Reality Fidelity (\(MAPE\)) - Validation
docs.text:
\[MAPE = \frac{100\%}{N} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \left| \frac{P_{sim,k} - P_{real,k}}{P_{real,k}} \right|\]
  • Role: Validates the accuracy of the digital twin (DynamicSimulatedSource) against the real SEPIC converter.
  • Replay Methodology: The recorded hardware duty sequence \(D(k)\) is replayed open-loop on the simulator configured with the measured I-V curve (MeasuredPanel), the matched step time (\(46\text{ ms}\)), and the actual load (\(50\ \Omega\)). Target: \(MAPE < 5\%\).

docs.title: 1.10. Two-Way ANOVA - Validation
docs.text:
• Role: Rigorous statistical hypothesis testing:
  • Factor A: Algorithm (P&O, InCond, Fuzzy, Scan&Track, PSO).
  • Factor B: Scenario (B1: Single Peak, B2: Partial Shading).
  • Dependent Variable: \(\eta_{ss}\) (or \(nRMSE\)).
  • Proves whether performance differences are statistically significant or attributable to bench noise (\(p < 0.05\)). See anova_analysis.md.

docs.title: 2. Deprioritized and Discarded Metrics
docs.text: Metric Status Reason for Deprioritization / Discard Static \(\eta\) (whole run) Secondary Conflates transient search and steady-state holding; sensitive to arbitrary run length. Power Ripple \(\Delta P_{pp}\) Secondary Limited by ADC sensor noise floor; subsumed by \(nRMSE\). Overshoot \(OS\) Secondary PV P-V curves are concave; power monotonically climbs unless flash irradiance occurs. Recomputed on the bench runs, \(OS\) is \(0.7\text{–}1.9\%\). docs.title: MPPT Algorithm Metrics Summary
docs.text: This document consolidates the full catalogue of metrics evaluated for the mpp-sdk project: their mathematical formulation, applicability, implementation status, and explicit selection for our comparative benchmark.

docs.title: 1. General Metrics Table & Selection
docs.text:
Selection legend:

  • Selected (Core): Primary metric used in the thesis / benchmark comparison.
  • Selected (Dynamic): Used in cyclic simulation.
  • Secondary: Calculable but redundant or noise-limited; used only as supporting diagnostic.
  • Discarded / Lab-Limited: Impracticable on our bench setup or formally discarded.
# Metric Symbol Formula Range / Unit Implementation Status Selection for Project Notes / Role in Benchmark 1 Static tracking efficiency \(\eta\) \(\displaystyle \frac{\langle P \rangle}{P_{mpp}} = \frac{1}{N \cdot P_{mpp}} \sum_{k=1}^{N} P_k\) \([0, 1]\) or \(\%\) Implemented Secondary Blends transient and steady state. Arbitrarily affected by run duration (\(10\text{ s}\) vs \(30\text{ s}\)). Use \(\eta_{ss} + E_{loss}\) instead. 2 Dynamic energy efficiency \(\eta_E\) \(\displaystyle \frac{\sum_{k=1}^N P_k}{\sum_{k=1}^N P_{mpp}(t_k)}\) \([0, 1]\) or \(\%\) Implemented Selected (Dynamic) Used in cyclic simulation (compare_cyclic.py), against the time-varying MPP of the profile. 3 Steady-state efficiency \(\eta_{ss}\) \(\displaystyle \frac{1}{M \cdot P_{mpp}} \sum_{k=N-M+1}^{N} P_k\) \([0, 1]\) or \(\%\) Implemented Selected (Core) Implemented as final_efficiency. Evaluates operating point quality after transients extinguish. 4 Settling / convergence time \(T_c\) (\(t_s\)) \(\displaystyle \min \{ t \mid \forall \tau \ge t, \, P(\tau) \ge (1 - \text{band}) P_{mpp} \}\) \([s]\) and steps Implemented Selected (Core) Measures initial lock speed. Report in both seconds and steps to bridge hardware (~46 ms) with sim (1 ms). 5 Peak-to-peak power ripple \(\Delta P_{pp}\) \(\displaystyle \max_{k \in \text{tail}} P_k - \min_{k \in \text{tail}} P_k\) \([W]\) Implemented Secondary Susceptible to sensor noise floor (0.07–0.17 W peak-to-peak over the tail in the bench runs). \(nRMSE\) is statistically superior for comparison. 6 Relative overshoot \(OS\) \(\displaystyle \frac{\max_k P_k - P_{settled}}{P_{settled}}\) \([0, \infty)\) or \(\%\) Implemented Secondary Non-physical for concave PV curves (bench values are \(0.7\text{–}1.9\%\)). 7 Local trap depth \(D_{trap}\) \(\displaystyle \frac{P_{settled}}{P_{global\_mpp}}\) \([0, 1]\) or \(\%\) Implemented Selected (Core) Decisive for Scenario 2 (partial shading). Cleanly separates local traps (~87-89%) from global tracking (~100%). 8 Steady-state RMSE \(RMSE\) \(\displaystyle \sqrt{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{k=N-M+1}^{N} (P_k - P_{mpp})^2}\) \([W]\) Planned Secondary Absolute dimensional error. Subsumed by normalized version (\(nRMSE\)). 9 Normalised RMSE \(nRMSE\) \(\displaystyle \frac{RMSE}{P_{mpp}} \times 100\%\) \(\%\) Planned Selected (Core) Penalizes oscillations quadratically and normalizes across different light levels (e.g. 7.7 W vs 4.3 W). 10 Mean absolute error \(MAE\) \(\displaystyle \frac{1}{M} \sum_{k=N-M+1}^{N} \| P_k - P_{mpp} \|\) \([W]\) Planned Secondary Linear tail error; highly collinear with \(nRMSE\). 11 Mean relative error \(RE\) \(\displaystyle \frac{1}{M} \sum_{k=N-M+1}^{N} \frac{\| P_k - P_{mpp} \|}{P_{mpp}} \times 100\%\) \(\%\) Planned Secondary Redundant with \(1 - \eta_{ss}\). Kept only as literature cross-reference. 12 Transient energy loss \(E_{loss}\) \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{T_c} (P_{mpp,k} - P_k) \cdot \Delta t\) \([J]\) Planned Selected (Core) Quantifies the exact energy cost of the search transient in Joules. Not available on our bench. See mppt_standards.md. 14 Global capture rate (GMPP hit rate) \(HR_{GMPP}\) \(\displaystyle \frac{N_{success}}{N_{attempts}} \times 100\%\) \([0, 100\%]\) Planned Selected (Core) Critical for global methods (PSO, Scan&Track). Evaluated over repeated runs under partial shading. 15 Simulation vs. real fidelity \(MAPE\) \(\displaystyle \frac{100\%}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \left\| \frac{P_{sim,k} - P_{real,k}}{P_{real,k}} \right\|\) \(\%\) Planned Selected (Validation) Replays recorded hardware \(D(k)\) through the digital twin (DynamicSimulatedSource). Target: \(< 5\%\). 16 Two-way analysis of variance \(ANOVA\) \(F_{alg}, F_{cond}, F_{int}, p\text{-value}\) Dimensionless Planned Selected (Validation) Statistical proof of significance across Algorithm × Condition (\(N \ge 5\) runs per cell). 17 Computational complexity per cycle \(t_{step}, Ops\) \(\displaystyle t_{exec} / \text{cycle}, \; \text{Flash/RAM}\) \([\mu s], [B]\) Planned Selected (Core) Evaluates feasibility on RP2040 MCU within 1 ms loop budget. docs.title: Standards for MPPT Evaluation
docs.text: Short reference list. Each entry was checked against the publisher's catalogue page. The standards themselves are not in the repo. Requirement tables and limits are not copied here: read the standard.

docs.title: EN 50530
docs.text:
• Title: Overall efficiency of grid connected photovoltaic inverters.
  • Edition: EN 50530:2010 with amendment A1:2013 (the current edition, as listed by BSI and DIN).
  • Scope: Test procedure for the efficiency of inverter MPPT, static and dynamic.
  • For this project: It tests an inverter with a PV simulator. We test an MPPT algorithm on a SEPIC converter with real panels and a lamp, so we only borrow the idea of static and dynamic MPPT efficiency.

docs.title: IEC 62891
docs.text:
• Title: Maximum power point tracking efficiency of grid connected photovoltaic inverters.
  • Edition: IEC 62891:2020, edition 1.0, published 2020-07-15.
  • Scope: Procedure to measure the MPPT efficiency of inverters in grid-connected PV systems. It treats static and dynamic MPPT efficiency separately.
  • For this project: Same limit as EN 50530: it needs a PV simulator with defined irradiance profiles. We only borrow the idea of an energy-weighted efficiency (energy_efficiency, see metrics_summary.md).

docs.title: ASTM E2848
docs.text:
• Title: Standard Test Method for Reporting Photovoltaic Non-Concentrator System Performance.
  • Edition: ASTM E2848-13 (2023), reapproved in 2023.
  • Scope: Capacity of an installed PV system under natural sunlight: acceptance testing, reporting of dc or ac performance, and monitoring over time. It reports power against reporting conditions of irradiance, ambient temperature and wind speed.
  • For this project: Does not apply. It is a plant-level method and it does not compare MPPT algorithms.

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• IEC 62816:2014 appeared in an earlier version of this page. No publisher page for it could be found, so it is not listed.
  • A comparison paper on MPPT standards was cited earlier. Its author and year could not be found, so it is dropped.
  • Femia, N. et al. (2017). Power Electronics and Control Techniques for Maximum Energy Harvesting in Photovoltaic Systems. CRC Press. Kept as a general reference on MPPT algorithms (not checked against a catalogue).

docs.title: Two-peak curves: algorithm comparison
docs.text:
Static simulation on measured curves. Not closed-loop bench runs.

  • Each algorithm runs 2000 steps on a measured I-V curve (MeasuredPanel behind a simulated SEPIC).
  • Curves are committed under data/bench/: B 60 and B 30 (10 Ohm session), B 45 (50 Ohm session).
  • Start duty is 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7. Seeds are fixed (PSO seed 0).
  • Efficiency is final power divided by the global peak of the curve.
  • "Global peak" is yes if final power is at least 98 % of the global peak.
  • "Steps" is the last step where power was more than 1 % from its final value. A value near 2000 means the algorithm never settled (it keeps scanning or dithering).
  • Final power and efficiency come from the last sample. For an algorithm that never settles (steps near 1999) the value is one point of an oscillation, not a steady value.
  • Peaks are local maxima of the measured samples. A hump that only comes from interpolation is not counted.
  • Regenerate with uv run python scripts/make_two_peak_results.py.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text:
Important limit: the valley between the two peaks is not measured. B 60 has no samples between 15.28 V and 30.38 V, B 30 none between 16.27 V and 32.54 V, and B 45 none between 15.99 V and 32.24 V. The algorithms see a straight line across this gap, so whether P&O "gets stuck" on the local peak depends on that interpolation.

On the 10 Ohm B 60 curve (sample peaks 4.75 W at 13.8 V and 6.35 W at 30.4 V), P&O, InCond and Fuzzy stop on the local peak at 4.74 W (74.6 to 74.8 % of the global peak) from all three start duties. Scan&Track and PSO find the global peak (98.7 and 98.8 %), but they do not settle inside 1 % in 2000 steps. B 30 is effectively single-peak: its only other sample peak is one point (1.82 W at 32.5 V) at the edge of the gap, against 4.74 W, so every algorithm ends at 100.0 % and it is not a real test. On the 50 Ohm B 45 curve the peaks are close (3.80 W and 4.03 W), so getting stuck costs only about 6 %. P&O, InCond and Fuzzy find the global peak from start duty 0.3 but end on the local one (94.3 to 94.4 %) from 0.5 and 0.7. Scan&Track and PSO find it from every start (100.0 and 99.9 %). Only B 60 has a clear gap, so this is a small sample. These are static simulations on measured curves, not closed-loop bench runs.
